Monitor for code with LLM generation artifacts such as uncommented blocks or unusual formatting consistency.

suggestion.title: LLM Prompt Injection & Sensitive Data Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Article implies 'leverage' of LLMs for attacks—threat actors likely inject prompts to extract sensitive data from model context; no detection UC for this exfiltration vector
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor HTTP POST bodies to ChatGPT/Gemini APIs for suspicious prompt keywords ('extract', 'dump', 'credentials', 'secrets', system prompt requests). Flag large text payloads (>1MB) followed by small responses. Correlate with user account compromise or insider activity.

suggestion.title: AI-Generated Phishing & Social Engineering Content Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states GREYVIBE 'leverage' LLMs 'to fuel cyberattacks'—strongly implies AI-crafted phishing emails or social engineering; no UC generated for this initial access vector
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect phishing emails with linguistic markers of LLM generation: unnatural phrasing, generic placeholders, unusual formatting consistency despite misspellings. Correlate with mass-mailing campaigns, anomalous sender reputation changes, and follow-up credential harvest attempts.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting from LLM Interaction Logs
suggestion.rationale: No detection UC for users accidentally pasting secrets into LLM chat interfaces, which attackers could then scrape or hijack to harvest credentials from exposed chat history
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor API requests to LLM services for embedded secrets (AWS keys, API tokens, DB connection strings) using high-confidence regex patterns. Alert on users sharing credentials in LLM chat sessions. Cross-reference with downstream unauthorized API/DB access events.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Installation from Non-Standard Registry
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes dependency confusion as the attack vector: malicious packages are pulled into build pipelines when resolution prefers attacker-controlled public npm registry. No detection exists to catch abnormal package sources.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install/yarn add operations that download packages from registries other than the organization's private registry or known approved public sources. Flag resolution of scoped packages (e.g., @company/module) from public npm when a private registry should exist. Baseline per-developer registry sources and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: npm Package PostInstall Script Executing System Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Article describes packages 'profile developer environments'—implied execution of system enumeration commands (uname, env, whoami, git config, AWS credential queries) during npm postinstall hooks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm/node processes spawning reconnaissance tools during package installation: env, git config, uname, aws sts, gcloud auth, hostname, whoami, id, ls on ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.kube. Look for sequential calls to multiple discovery commands from a single npm postinstall context. Monitor for process creation with npm parent and suspicious command-line args.

suggestion.title: npm Package Making Outbound Connections During Installation
suggestion.rationale: Dependency confusion attack requires exfiltrating reconnaissance data to attacker infrastructure. Article implies data collection flows back to attacker: '...collect reconnaissance data...' implies command-and-control or exfiltration endpoint.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for network connections initiated by npm or node processes during package installation phase (within first 60 seconds of npm install). Flag HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains not in allow-list. Correlate outbound connections with environment variable exfiltration patterns in URL queries or POST bodies containing system info (OS version, hostname, user, git email).

suggestion.title: npm Package Accessing Developer Credential Files
suggestion.rationale: Reconnaissance objective logically includes credential harvesting. Article scope 'developer environments' implies access attempts to ~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.git-credentials, GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN environment variables during package execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect npm/node process reading from credential-bearing paths or environment variables: ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.git-credentials, .netrc, env vars matching *TOKEN, *KEY, *SECRET, *PASSWORD. Cross-reference file access timestamps with npm install activity. Alert on any credential file read by postinstall scripts.

suggestion.title: Multiple Malicious npm Packages From Same Upstream Source
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 33 packages in single campaign. Dependency confusion exploits typically distribute multiple malicious packages to maximize hit rate across different projects. Detection should cluster by source IP, domain, or publishing account.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate npm package downloads across a organization over 7-day window. Cluster packages by source IP or domain of origin (registry). Alert if >3 unique packages originate from the same non-standard registry or source IP, especially for packages with <100 total downloads industry-wide or published within days of each other by new accounts.

suggestion.title: npm Package with Suspicious PostInstall Script Obfuscation
suggestion.rationale: Malicious npm packages hide reconnaissance logic. Article implies payload is encoded/obfuscated in postinstall scripts to evade static analysis during 'npm install' phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Inspect package.json postinstall/preinstall scripts for obfuscation indicators: base64 encoding, hex-encoded strings, JavaScript eval() calls, process.env access chains, shell-escaped quoting patterns, or curl/wget downloading external payloads. Flag packages where script length exceeds 500 chars or contains >3 obfuscation markers. Cross-check against npm registry manifest signatures if available.

suggestion.title: GlobalProtect Portal Authentication Bypass — Unauthenticated Access
suggestion.rationale: Article title indicates authentication bypass under active exploitation. No use cases were generated to detect unauthenticated access to protected GlobalProtect resources. Detection should flag POST requests to GlobalProtect API endpoints that succeed without valid session tokens or MFA.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP 200 responses to GlobalProtect portal endpoints (/ssl-vpn/) from external sources without corresponding prior authentication handshakes. Alert on successful requests bearing no sessionid cookie or with invalid/expired tokens. Baseline legitimate remote access patterns and deviation from baseline.

suggestion.title: Post-Bypass Lateral Movement — Authenticated Portal Command Execution
suggestion.rationale: Exploitation of authentication bypass typically chains to reconnaissance, credential theft, or lateral movement. Pipeline generated no use cases for detecting attacker actions *after* successful bypass. Should detect abnormal administrative commands or privilege escalation within PAN-OS console post-bypass.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on admin API calls (e.g., /api/index.php actions) or CLI commands executed immediately after a successful CVE-2026-0257 bypass attempt. Flag admin user creation, configuration export, or firewall rule modifications from IPs that previously failed authentication. Watch for non-interactive admin sessions or concurrent admin logins.

suggestion.title: PAN-OS GlobalProtect Portal Version Fingerprinting — Exploitation Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Attackers exploit version-specific CVEs. Pipeline missed detection for reconnaissance probes targeting GlobalProtect version disclosure endpoints. No use case exists to flag version-detection requests (e.g., /global-protect/login.esp, version headers).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect repeated requests to GlobalProtect endpoints known to leak version information (User-Agent parsing, banner-grab attempts, or requests to /global-protect/login.esp from external IPs). Flag scanning patterns with rotating User-Agents or automated tools probing for CVE-2026-0257 signatures.

suggestion.title: Suspicious GlobalProtect Portal File Uploads — Backdoor Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Authentication bypass chains often lead to backdoor implantation. Pipeline generated no use cases for detecting malicious file uploads to GlobalProtect endpoints or configuration directories. Missing detection for unauthorized writes to portal directories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on PUT/POST requests to GlobalProtect portal directories (/global-protect/, /admin/) containing binary payloads or script files (.aspx, .jsp, .php, .sh) from non-administrative sources. Flag any successful file writes to GlobalProtect config or plugin directories post-bypass.

suggestion.title: Encrypted VPN Tunnel Anomaly — Exfiltration Over Compromised GlobalProtect
suggestion.rationale: Successful authentication bypass grants attacker VPN access. Pipeline generated no use cases for detecting abnormal encrypted tunnel activity (data volume, destinations, or protocol anomalies) post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unusual tunnel egress patterns post-bypass: sustained high-volume encrypted traffic to non-corporate destinations, tunneled command-and-control callbacks, or protocols typically blocked (SSH, RDP) transiting through established GlobalProtect sessions from external IPs previously detected in bypass attempts.

suggestion.title: Developer Tooling Credential Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly addresses 'exfiltrate source code and secrets' via 'trusted developer tooling'—core threat vector not detected by pipeline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for exfiltration of secrets and source code repositories via developer tools (git, npm, pip). Flag outbound HTTPS/SSH traffic from git/package-manager processes to non-canonical external hosts or cloud storage services. Correlate with large file egress from .git, .env, or source-tree directories.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Compromise via Trusted Developer Tools
suggestion.rationale: Title references 'trusted developer tooling'—indicates supply-chain or dependency-substitution attack that pipeline did not reconstruct.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unexpected modifications to developer tool configs (npm .npmrc, pip requirements.txt, .git/config) or installation of packages/tools from untrusted repositories. Alert on execution of third-party build scripts or package setup scripts with elevated privileges.

suggestion.title: Reconnaissance and Enumeration of Developer Secrets
suggestion.rationale: Exfiltration of secrets requires prior discovery—article's threat model implies enumeration of credential stores that pipeline missed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for enumeration and reads of secret-storage locations (.env, .kube/config, .aws/credentials, .ssh, API-key files). Flag recursive directory traversals of source trees or bulk-reading of configuration files by developer-tool processes.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement Using Compromised Developer Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Compromised developer tooling often contains SSH keys and auth tokens used for cross-system access—not addressed in empty kill chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track reuse of developer SSH keys, git authentication tokens, or package-manager credentials across multiple systems or from atypical source IPs. Alert on git operations to internal infrastructure or over non-standard SSH ports from compromised workstations.

suggestion.title: Abuse of Package Manager for Malicious Dependency Injection
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain abuse of developer tooling commonly involves package-manager compromise; title implies this but pipeline reconstructed zero phases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect invocation of package managers (npm, pip, dotnet, gradle) with flags that bypass integrity checks (--no-verify, --skip-scripts). Flag unexpected package installation or modification in build pipelines, especially those pulling from non-canonical sources or with suspicious post-install scripts.

suggestion.title: Marimo CVE-2026-39987 Exploitation Attempt Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly names 'Marimo CVE-2026-39987 Exploit' as the attack vector; this is the initial access. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs and missed this entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP requests to Marimo endpoints with payloads triggering CVE-2026-39987 (likely involving deserialization or code-injection in reactive notebook parameters). Correlate with unexpected child processes spawned from Marimo Python interpreter.

suggestion.title: LLM Agent–Driven Post-Exploitation Command Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title identifies 'LLM Agent for Post-Exploitation' as the primary attack mechanism; no use cases generated for LLM-driven execution despite being the headline attack differentiator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect command-line payloads with high Shannon entropy, unusual whitespace/argument ordering, or embedded base64/hex encoding—signatures of LLM-generated commands. Escalate if command parent is Python, Marimo process, or LLM inference runtime.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Discovery from Marimo Execution Context
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attack sequence as 'after exploit'; reconnaissance and system-enumeration steps must follow code execution. Pipeline did not map this discovery phase.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag rapid-fire execution of system enumeration binaries (whoami, id, uname, systeminfo, net.exe, tasklist, ps) with parent being Marimo or LLM-spawned processes. LLM agents typically gather OS/environment data before lateral movement or exfiltration.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Python Child Process Creation from Marimo
suggestion.rationale: CVE-2026-39987 exploitation would grant code execution in Marimo's Python context; post-exploitation typically spawns additional processes. Not captured in empty kill chain.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Python child processes (subprocess.Popen, os.system, exec) spawned by Marimo parent, especially with arguments from user-controlled notebook cells or LLM-generated payloads.

suggestion.title: Vishing-Triggered Entra Account Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'voice phishing (vishing) attack that compromised an employee's Microsoft Entra account.' No detection logic captured this initial access vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag sign-in events from employee's Entra account within 24-48 hours post-vishing campaign. Correlate with MFA failures, unusual geography, and subsequent privileged API calls. Monitor for new device registration or bypass of conditional access policies.

suggestion.title: Salesforce Mass Data Export by Compromised Entra Identity
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'used this access to steal 42 million records from the company's Salesforce instance, including consumer and business customer names, email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers.' No UC detected this lateral-movement-to-exfiltration pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on bulk Salesforce record exports (>10k rows) originating from recently-compromised service accounts. Correlate with unusual API quota consumption, off-hours export timestamps, and export destinations not in baseline IP space.

suggestion.title: Dark Web Leak Site Publication of Exfiltrated SaaS Data
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'After the company refused to pay the ransom... the cybercrime group leaked the documents stolen from Charter's Salesforce instance on their dark web leak site.' No detection for extortion-campaign monitoring or leak-site indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference exfiltrated data artifacts (file hashes, record samples from Have I Been Pwned analysis) against organization's data fingerprints. Alert on publication of 4.9M+ unique email/phone records matching customer database schema.

suggestion.title: ShinyHunters Salesforce-Targeting Campaign Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article notes: 'ShinyHunters has been targeting Salesforce customers over the past year, breaching hundreds of companies worldwide.' Pipeline missed actor-specific TTP pattern across vertical.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain ShinyHunters actor profile with known vishing scripts, social-engineering pretexts, and Salesforce admin/developer targeting patterns. Flag employees matching typical targets (Salesforce admins, customer-success roles, finance leads handling customer data).

suggestion.title: Ransom Demand Communication from ShinyHunters Extortion Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and told BleepingComputer that they breached the company's systems on April 1.' Impact phase—ransom demand—generated no alerting logic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for communications from ShinyHunters infrastructure (known email addresses, Tor endpoints, leak-site URLs). Cross-reference with exfiltration timeline. Alert on ransom notes or extortion language containing specific data samples proving breach access.

suggestion.title: Account Discovery & Reconnaissance in Compromised Salesforce Environment
suggestion.rationale: Article implies post-breach exploration: '42 million records from the company's Salesforce instance, including... support ticket data.' Pipeline missed reconnaissance phase within SaaS environment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid enumeration of Salesforce objects, report generation sprees, or bulk-query patterns from single service-account origin post-compromise. Flag access to administrative dashboards or customer-data reports by recently-activated accounts.

suggestion.title: ChatGPT Web Summary Feature Abuse - Malicious URL Summarization
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly establishes 'ChatGPT Web Summaries' as the phishing surface ('Turns ChatGPT Web Summaries Into a Phishing Surface'), but pipeline generated zero use cases for detecting this attack vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor ChatGPT API calls and web UI access to the summarization feature for requests targeting known phishing domains, credential harvesting sites, or newly registered domains. Alert on summarization requests from the same IP/account to multiple distinct phishing-category domains within short time windows.

suggestion.title: Unusual ChatGPT Summarization Pattern - Potential Phishing Reconnaissance
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline did not map reconnaissance phase. Attacker likely uses summarization feature to test/refine phishing pages before sending—this behavioral pattern is missing entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid, repeated summarization requests to similar-looking domains (edit distance < 3) or domains with high phishing-kit similarity (same hosting provider, similar TLD patterns). Flag accounts that summarize pages containing credential entry forms.

suggestion.title: ChatGPT Summary Content Injection - Phishing Form Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states summaries are used as phishing surface, implying attacker-controlled content appears in summaries. No detection for phishing indicators (form fields, urgency language, spoofed branding) embedded in summarized output.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor ChatGPT summary output (via API logs or session recording) for presence of HTML form tags, password input fields, or phishing keywords ('verify account', 'confirm identity', 'urgent action') in the summarized text. Cross-reference summarized URLs against phishing databases.

suggestion.title: Cross-Origin Phishing Redirect via ChatGPT Summary Links
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline missed the likelihood that attacker uses ChatGPT summaries to legitimize/redirect to phishing pages. No detection for chain: user clicks link in summary → phishing landing page.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate clicks on ChatGPT summary result links with subsequent redirects to phishing infrastructure. Flag if the final destination domain differs significantly from the summarized domain (SSRF-like pattern). Alert on multiple users clicking the same malicious summary link.

suggestion.title: ChatGPT Account Compromise - Mass Summarization of Phishing URLs
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline ignored the scenario where a compromised ChatGPT account is used to generate summaries at scale. No detection for bulk/automated summarization activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect sudden spike in summarization API calls from a single account or API key, especially if originating from new IP or unusual geolocation. Alert on summarization requests to a cohort of phishing-category domains in short succession (>50 unique URLs in 10 minutes).

suggestion.title: ChatGPT Vulnerability Exploitation - CVE Indicator Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title indicates this is a named vulnerability ('ChatGPhish Vulnerability'), which should map to a CVE. Pipeline extracted no CVE identifier, domain names, or proof-of-concept indicators despite 'CRIT' severity tag.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for CVE-2024-XXXXX (ChatGPhish) exploitation attempts, including unusual summarization API parameters, malformed requests to web summary endpoints, or unauthenticated calls to the feature. Alert on API response codes indicating successful exploitation (200 OK with unexpected summary format).

suggestion.title: Suspicious ChatGPT Desktop Application Download
suggestion.rationale: Article describes fake outage page with download prompt directing users to openew[.]app impersonating OpenAI: 'If the visitor clicks on the download button, they are brought to a website at openew[.]app that impersonates OpenAI's desktop application download portal.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on downloads of .exe or .dmg files with 'ChatGPT' in filename from non-OpenAI domains. Cross-reference user navigation paths: fake outage pages (especially on chatgpt.com/s/*) immediately followed by downloads from suspicious domains indicate targeted lure exploitation.

suggestion.title: OpenAI Domain Impersonation Download Site
suggestion.rationale: The malware delivery endpoint is explicitly identified: 'The website offers both macOS and Windows downloads that install malware on devices.' The domain openew[.]app is typosquatting/impersonating the legitimate OpenAI infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Block/alert on downloads from domains matching 'openew', 'opene[w]', or similar OpenAI typosquats. Flag binary downloads from such sites regardless of filename or User-Agent string claiming to be from legitimate applications.

suggestion.title: Malicious Content in ChatGPT Shared Conversations
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'The attackers created a custom HTML page using ChatGPT's rendering capabilities and published it through a shared chatgpt.com/s/ link, allowing the fake outage notice to be displayed from a legitimate ChatGPT URL.' Detection must identify when legitimate platforms host phishing/social engineering content.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor traffic to chatgpt.com/s/* URLs and identify those containing outage-related messaging, download prompts, or service impersonation language. Correlate with subsequent downloads and Google Ads referrers to identify social engineering chains.

suggestion.title: Virtual Machine Detection in Installer Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly documents evasion behavior: 'BleepingComputer's test of the Windows version on Any.Run found that it executes various commands to determine whether the device is a legitimate computer or a virtual machine.' This VM fingerprinting is characteristic of malware evasion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag process creation events where suspicious installers or unsigned executables execute commands querying CPUID, SMBIOS, registry keys (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System), or WMI classes that enumerate hypervisor presence. Alert on combinations of installer execution + VM detection commands.

suggestion.title: Infostealer Execution Post-Installer
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates payload type: 'While it is unclear what payloads are ultimately deployed, earlier campaigns abusing AI platform sharing features have distributed infostealers.' The malware family is credential/data theft focused.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Following suspicious ChatGPT installer execution, alert on child processes accessing browser credential stores (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome, %APPDATA%\Mozilla), password manager configuration files, or registry keys containing saved credentials. Monitor for unusual network exfiltration from the installer process.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-0257 Vulnerable Asset Inventory Triage
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'match against your vulnerability scanner' and emphasizes 'patch lag is the silent killer'. CISA KEV classification means active wild exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query all vulnerability scanners (Qualys, Nessus, Rapid7, Tenable) for CVE-2026-0257 detections on PAN-OS instances. Cross-reference with asset inventory to identify exposed devices. Prioritize any instance unpatched by federal deadline 2026-06-01. Correlate with network egress rules and internet routing tables to flag internet-facing assets.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized VPN Authentication Bypass Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes capability to 'establish an unauthorized VPN connection'. Auth bypass exploits target VPN establishment as primary impact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor PAN-OS VPN logs for successful IPSec/SSL-VPN sessions without corresponding preauthentication records. Flag VPN connections from unexpected geographies, suspicious service accounts, or off-hours access. Alert on session establishment followed immediately by administrative activity or policy queries.

suggestion.title: PAN-OS Management Interface Unauthorized Access Post-Auth Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'allows attackers to bypass security restrictions', implying unauthorized admin-plane access via authentication bypass of management interface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on successful PAN-OS admin logins (GUI or API) from untrusted IPs without corresponding successful pre-authentication events. Monitor for admin access outside business hours or from high-risk geographies. Correlate failed authentication attempts followed by successful session establishment (auth bypass signature).

suggestion.title: Externally Exposed PAN-OS Management Interface Discovery
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'KEV implies active exploitation against exposed assets'. Publicly routable management interfaces are exploitation prerequisites; attackers scan for exposure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Execute network scans on public IP space for PAN-OS management interfaces (identify via TLS cert subject CN, HTTP banner, admin login page signature). Cross-reference asset CMDB. Flag any internet-routable PAN-OS device; prioritize unpatched instances per vulnerability scan. Validate exposure with external tools (Shodan, Censys API).

suggestion.title: Post-Breach Lateral Movement via Compromised VPN Sessions
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attacker capability to establish VPN connection post-bypass. Detect internal reconnaissance and lateral movement originating from unauthorized VPN sessions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate authenticated VPN sessions with subsequent lateral movement patterns. Flag internal DNS queries and port scanning activity from VPN-sourced IPs. Monitor for connections to administrative endpoints (domain controllers, privileged jump boxes) from compromised VPN session IPs.

suggestion.title: PAN-OS Configuration Tampering and Audit Trail Suppression
suggestion.rationale: Unauthorized admin access post-auth bypass will lead to policy modification and potential audit disablement. Detect suspicious configuration changes and logging framework tampering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor PAN-OS configuration change audit trail for commits from non-administrator accounts or unexpected sources. Alert on deletion/disablement of logging, audit rules, or threat prevention signatures. Flag modifications to admin user accounts, API keys, or authentication bypass rules.

suggestion.title: Residential Proxy Service C2 Communication Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes botnet using 200 servers to control millions of devices via proxy service for command and control; no UC created to detect anomalous outbound connections from consumer devices to known C2 infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify consumer devices (non-server OS) establishing outbound connections to hosting provider IPs at patterns inconsistent with normal user behavior. Look for sustained or repeating connections to IP space linked to residential proxy infrastructure or hosting providers known to host botnet C2.

suggestion.title: Botnet-Driven DDoS Attack Origin Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states botnet was used 'to carry out cyberattacks' including distributed denial-of-service; no UC created to detect inbound DDoS traffic from residential IP ranges or identify victim perspective anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for high-volume, synchronized traffic floods originating from dispersed residential IP addresses. Correlate source IPs against known residential proxy provider IP ranges. Flag traffic patterns consistent with botnet-coordinated attacks (short duration, high concurrency, multiple geographic origins).

suggestion.title: Cryptocurrency Mining Activity on Infected Consumer Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'cryptocurrency mining' as explicit use case for botnet; no UC created to detect pool connections, excessive CPU utilization, or mining-specific traffic patterns from consumer endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect sustained connections from consumer devices to known cryptocurrency mining pools. Monitor for unusual process CPU consumption patterns on non-server devices. Identify stratum protocol handshakes or Monero/Bitcoin miner process execution on infected endpoints.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Proxy Service Configuration on Managed Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article describes Asocks platform advertising '150 locations, 100,000 clients' and offering bulk subscription discounts; infection mechanism involves device compromise. Detection should flag unexpected proxy client installation or configuration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on installation of known residential proxy clients (Asocks agent, similar malware) on endpoints. Monitor for suspicious registry/config changes enabling proxy functionality without user consent. Track child processes of common downloaders executing proxy client installers.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Outbound Traffic from Consumer Devices to Hosting Providers
suggestion.rationale: Article notes seized servers were 'located in the Netherlands' at a local hosting provider; infected devices established persistent C2 to these IPs. Detection should identify consumer endpoints with sustained outbound traffic to non-residential hosting provider IP space.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify consumer devices with persistent outbound connections to datacenter/hosting provider ASNs (especially Netherlands-based providers). Correlate with known C2 infrastructure. Flag high volume or long-duration connections inconsistent with normal user activity.

suggestion.title: Weak Device Credential Exploitation in Botnet Infection Context
suggestion.rationale: Article's protective guidance states 'ensure the default credentials have been changed,' implying infection vector included default credential abuse on networking devices; no UC created for detection of credential-based compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for successful authentication to networking devices or service interfaces using default credentials (admin/admin, admin/12345, etc.). Flag repeated failed login attempts followed by success on consumer-grade routers or IoT devices. Alert on unexpected geographic origin of device administration logins.

suggestion.title: vm2 sandbox-escape PoC signature strings in HTTP traffic/WAF
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly documents PoC using Buffer.call.call, __lookupGetter__, __lookupSetter__ as attack primitives. Article states: 'vm2 sandbox-escape PoC strings observed in inbound HTTP request body / WAF' with reference strings: Buffer.call.call, __lookupGetter__, __lookupSetter__, compileStreaming, mainModule.require, constructor.constructor.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP requests (inbound to Node.js applications) containing any of the documented exploit-string signatures. These strings have no legitimate use in normal web traffic and strongly indicate sandbox-escape exploitation attempt.

suggestion.title: Node.js spawning unexpected OS shells immediately post-exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article PoC results in code execution capability. Article states this attack enables: 'run arbitrary code' and detection should hunt 'Node.exe spawning OS shell after vm2 sandbox exploitation' with process indicators like child_process and execSync.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Node process (node.exe, node.js) spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, sh, or wmic with command lines containing child_process, execSync, or echo patterns. Indicates post-sandbox-escape arbitrary code execution being weaponized into shell access.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable vm2 versions (≤3.11.3) in software inventory
suggestion.rationale: Vulnerability is version-specific. Article state: 'Vulnerable vm2 package (<=3.11.3) present in Defender software inventory' as a recommended hunt. Provides asset-level risk stratification independent of exploitation evidence.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query asset inventory for npm package 'vm2' with SoftwareVersion matching regex ^([0-2]\.|3\.([0-9]|10|11)(\.\d)?$) to identify all systems running unpatched versions. Cross-reference with exposed Node.js services.

suggestion.title: vm2 Module Instantiation with Sandbox Bypass Pattern — CVE-2026-47137 exploitation attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes the vulnerability: 'strict equality (`options.require === false`), which is trivially bypassed by omitting the `require` option entirely... When `require` is not specified, `options.require` is `undefined`.' No UC detects suspicious vm2 code patterns or instantiation configurations (nesting:true + implicit require). This is the actual exploitation mechanism, not the post-exploitation artifacts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for Node.js process command-line arguments or source code patterns containing vm2 instantiation with nesting:true and no explicit require:false option. Look for code patterns like `new NodeVM({nesting:true})` without accompanying require restrictions. This detects the actual vulnerability condition before exploitation completes.

suggestion.title: Node.js Application Exposing vm2 via Web Endpoint — CVE-2026-47137 web-based attack surface
suggestion.rationale: Article lists T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) as a technique but no UC addresses web-based exploitation. Vulnerable vm2 instances are often exposed via Express/Koa endpoints for code evaluation or sandboxing features. Article does not specify deployment context but T1190 strongly implies public-facing exposure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for HTTP requests to Node.js applications with payloads attempting sandbox escape (nesting:true parameter values, require-bypass patterns in POST/GET params). Correlate with Node.js process spawning of shells following suspicious HTTP requests. Focus on endpoints known to use vm2 (code-execution APIs, REPL services, sandbox tools).

suggestion.title: Parent Process Tree Anomaly — Node.js spawning shells without process hierarchy precedent
suggestion.rationale: Article describes RCE via sandbox escape but no UC validates whether the shell-spawning Node.js process is itself suspicious (e.g., service/daemon process escalating to interactive shell vs. dev tool legitimately orchestrating builds). UC_20_2 looks for the shell spawn but lacks parent-context filtering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Refine UC_20_2 to filter on Node.js parent processes that are unexpected for shell invocation: system services (svchost, systemd), Node.js app servers without build/deploy context, daemons running vm2 in production sandbox mode. Exclude developers running node from shell directly or npm build scripts. Baseline legitimate node→shell patterns per environment.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-47140 vm2 vulnerable version inventory
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly lists under 'Indicators of Compromise: CVE-2026-47140' and describes affected versions (NodeVM <3.11.4). This is reconnaissance/weapon phase—required to detect hosts vulnerable before exploitation. No pipeline use case generated despite clear attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Surface installed vm2 npm package versions matching vulnerable range (^3\.[0-9]|3\.10|3\.11\.[0-3]) via package.json inventory or process/module enumeration. Correlate DeviceInfo for internet-facing exposure and prior NodeVM activity.

suggestion.title: NodeVM process and inspector/promises module bypass detection
suggestion.rationale: Article's core vulnerability statement: denylist 'misses process and inspector/promises. Both can be used from sandboxed code to reach host-side execution primitives.' These ARE the exploit vectors—article explicitly names the bypass method. Pipeline generated zero use cases for this critical technique.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect require() calls or command-line arguments containing 'inspector/promises', 'getBuiltinModule', or 'process.binding()' from node.exe context. Look for these strings in process arguments or .js files created outside node_modules. Flag especially when combined with NodeVM framework references.

suggestion.title: Host command execution from Node.js sandbox escape
suggestion.rationale: Article describes endpoint: 'sandboxed code to bypass builtin restrictions and execute code in the host process.' This is the impact phase—process spawning (cmd/powershell/bash) from NodeVM context. Article names specific shells in techniques (T1059.001/003/007) but pipeline generated no execution detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect child processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, bash, sh) spawned from node.exe where parent command context contains 'vm2', 'NodeVM', or suspicious JavaScript execution. Flag user context mismatch (e.g., SYSTEM child from user-mode node parent).

suggestion.title: Malicious JavaScript deployment for NodeVM exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article technique T1204.002 (User Execution: Malicious File) implies attacker delivers exploit payload as .js file. Article describes code must use 'process' and 'inspector/promises' to bypass. Pipeline missed detection for suspicious .js artifact creation/execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect .js/.mjs/.cjs file creation in suspicious paths (temp, Downloads, AppData, web-cache) followed by execution via node.exe. Correlate creation source (email attachment, web download path). Flag files created seconds before node execution.

suggestion.title: Execution guardrails circumvention via builtin module reflection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly lists T1480 (Execution Guardrails) as technique. The denylist itself IS the guardrail being circumvented. Article states 'blocks several dangerous builtins...However, the denylist misses process and inspector/promises.' This is guardrail evasion. No pipeline detection for this bypass pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Node.js processes running NodeVM/vm2 context (module references, vm.runInNewContext patterns) that attempt to load or call restricted modules via reflection (getBuiltinModule, require.resolve, binding() calls). Flag as sandbox-escape indicator.

suggestion.title: Defense evasion via denylist bypass introspection
suggestion.rationale: Article technique T1211 (Exploitation for Defense Evasion) directly addresses that the bypass itself is evasion—circumventing the security control (builtin denylist) IS the defense-evasion step. Separate from execution; notable pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for introspection attempts within Node.js: require.cache enumeration, process.binding calls, or Object.getOwnPropertyNames(process) patterns. These are fingerprinting the sandbox. Correlate with subsequent module-loading attempts to identify active bypass attempts.

suggestion.title: WebAssembly JSPI Promise.finally() exploitation in vm2 context
suggestion.rationale: Article core threat: 'JSPI-backed Promise can reach Promise.prototype.finally() in a way that bypasses the expected Promise-species hardening and exposes a host-originate[d context]'. No detection for WebAssembly.Suspending/WebAssembly.promising runtime state or Promise species override during async code execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Node.js processes with vm2 module loaded executing async code that then spawns shell or accesses host resources. Secondary indicator: process command lines or source code containing 'Promise.finally()' or async/await patterns immediately preceding host process escape. Tertiary: network connections initiated from vm2 context (C2 from broken sandbox).

suggestion.title: vm2 sandbox boundary escape to host filesystem
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'arbitrary code execution in the host process' (T1611). Technique is listed but no detection for the escape itself—only post-exploitation. Gap: detecting when vm2-sandboxed code accesses files outside sandbox boundary.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Within Node.js process with active vm2 context, detect file-access (read/write/modify) to paths outside intended sandbox: parent-directory traversal (../../../), system paths (/etc, /proc, /var, HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE), or host node_modules outside the vm2 instance's module path.

suggestion.title: Promise constructor or .finally() prototype manipulation in vm2 runtime
suggestion.rationale: Article root cause: species hardening bypass via Promise.prototype.finally() manipulation. No detection for JavaScript prototype-chain tampering or constructor override within vm2 vm.run() execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate vm2 module invocation with subsequent process spawns within 1-5 seconds (indicating successful sandbox break-out via Promise exploit). Alternative: elevated DeviceProcessEvents for Node.js followed by child-process creation at host privilege level when vm2 expected unprivileged context.

suggestion.title: Untrusted input execution in vm2 with async and JSPI-capable configuration
suggestion.rationale: Article precondition: 'untrusted code is executed with async support on runtimes exposing WebAssembly JSPI'. Detection should flag configuration and input combination that creates exploitability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline Node.js applications using vm2 by safe parameters (no async, no JSPI). Alert on: vm2 vm.run() calls with async code paths enabled (asyncContextExtended=true or similar), combined with dynamic/external input sources (HTTP endpoints, file uploads, stdin).

suggestion.title: vm2 package version drift or unsafe version in active use
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies vulnerable versions ≤3.11.3. No proactive hunt for version pinning or version inventory beyond file presence (UC_19_3). Should detect when safe version is declared but unsafe version is actually loaded.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Compare vm2 package.json declared version against actual require() load path at runtime. Flag when package-lock.json or yarn.lock specifies safe version (≥3.11.4) but process loads vulnerable version from alternative path (old node_modules, global npm cache, devDependencies override).

suggestion.title: [EXEC] Python eval() invocation in PraisonAI tool/plugin code
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states vulnerability is 'registers a `calculate(expression)` tool implemented with Python `eval(expression)`'. This is the execution vector; no detection exists for eval() patterns in tool definitions or plugins.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for modifications to PraisonAI tool/plugin Python files containing eval() patterns. Monitor DeviceFileEvents for .py files under praisonai/tools/ or custom plugin directories with eval() in the diff. Cross-correlate with process execution events where the parent python/uvicorn process accepts external network input.

suggestion.title: [CONFIG] PraisonAI A2A configuration missing auth_token
suggestion.rationale: Article states the root cause is 'example exposes an A2A server without configuring `auth_token`'. No detection targets missing authentication controls explicitly.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for PraisonAI startup without auth_token in argv, environment variables, or config files. Flag config files (app.yml, .env, config.py) that define A2A server parameters but lack auth_token entries. Correlate with network listen events on high-numbered ports.

suggestion.title: [EXPOSE] Uvicorn/Python process binding 0.0.0.0 with external traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes the service 'binds the server to `0.0.0.0`' alongside unauthenticated access. Network-level exposure hunt separate from HTTP-layer detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for Python/Uvicorn processes with listening sockets on 0.0.0.0:8000, 0.0.0.0:8080, or standard HTTP ports accepting inbound traffic from non-RFC1918 sources. Correlate with command-line absence of --ssl-* flags or authentication middleware to identify unprotected bindings.

suggestion.title: [ATTACK] LLM-generated dynamic subprocess execution post-eval()
suggestion.rationale: Kill chain combines LLM tool selection + eval() execution + subprocess spawning. Article describes eval() reaching 'real LLM-driven tool execution'; need detection for the full chain from input parsing to shell command execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for process trees where parent=python/uvicorn with a2a/praisonai in command-line spawns child sh/bash/cmd.exe with suspicious arguments (system info, file access, credential enumeration). Baseline: legitimate process spawning should have predictable patterns; LLM-driven execution will show random/diverse command arguments.

suggestion.title: [REPO] PraisonAI official vulnerable example code clone/checkout
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'official example' paths. Detection needed to catch deployment of the vulnerable example repository structure itself.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for presence of PraisonAI repository under common git clone paths (~/.cache/pip/, ~/projects/, /opt/) with the vulnerable a2a-server.py example executable and running. Flag if example code is ever executed in production context (non-sandbox environment).

suggestion.title: [NET] HTTP POST to /a2a with JSON-RPC structure (method + params pattern)
suggestion.rationale: Article describes attack vector as 'JSON-RPC POST' to /a2a endpoint. Need detection for the specific JSON-RPC protocol structure to distinguish from benign /a2a traffic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for HTTP POST requests to /a2a endpoints where request body contains JSON-RPC structure ("jsonrpc", "method", "params" keys). Particularly flag requests with method values like 'evaluate', 'execute', 'calculate', or 'run' originating from non-internal networks without valid auth headers.

suggestion.title: [High-Fidelity] Python attribute introspection: `__self__`, `__dict__`, `__class__` chains in restricted context
suggestion.rationale: Article core attack: 'print.__self__ to retrieve the real Python builtins module'. Should detect attribute-chaining on builtin callables (print, open, etc.) that access __self__ or __dict__ or __class__, which is unusual and specific to sandbox-escape exploits.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Python process command lines and script files for patterns matching object.__self__, object.__dict__, or object.__class__ chains, especially when the base object is a builtin function. Pair with context showing restricted execution (venv, subprocess, execute_code function). Regex: (\w+)\.__self__ or (\w+)\.__dict__\[['"](\w+)['"]\].

suggestion.title: [Behavioral] Sequential discovery + credential-access in subprocess context
suggestion.rationale: Article hunts show commands: 'id', 'whoami', 'uname -a', 'hostname', then 'env', 'printenv', 'cat /etc/passwd', credential keys. Should detect rapid sequence of discovery (T1087, T1518) followed by credential-reading (T1552) from Python subprocess spawned by PraisonAI.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate Python-spawned shell processes executing discovery commands (whoami, id, uname, hostname, env, printenv) immediately followed by sensitive-file or credential-variable reads (/etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, AWS_*, AZURE_*, OPENAI_*, /run/secrets). Time delta < 5 seconds, same shell PID.

suggestion.title: [Medium-Fidelity] `vars()` + `__import__` reconstruction in Python subprocess
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies exploit extracts '__import__ via vars() and runtime string construction'. Should detect code attempting to dynamically reconstruct __import__ by accessing vars() on builtins or using string concatenation to build forbidden function names.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for Python command lines containing both 'vars(' AND '__import__' (including obfuscations like '__imp' + 'ort' or '__' + 'import' or encoded variants). Require parent context showing execute_code, praisonai, or sandbox keyword. Lower threshold for file-write detections of .py files containing these patterns.

suggestion.title: [Behavioral] subprocess module + builtins namespace leak detection
suggestion.rationale: Sandbox-escape exploits often work by accessing builtins dict from restricted code. Should detect subprocess-spawned code that imports builtins, accesses __dict__ on modules, or uses getattr on print/open.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Python code containing 'import builtins' or 'from builtins import' in subprocess context, or getattr(print, '__self__'), or [x for x in dir() if '__' in x], or similar metaclass/introspection patterns. These are red flags for sandbox escape attempts.

suggestion.title: praisonai Package Installation or Import
suggestion.rationale: Article states users 'follow the documented quickstart' and deploy via `praisonai deploy --type api`. Pipeline should detect package installation/import: 'emits a Flask server' implies praisonai module presence. No UC covers pip install or Python import hooks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect pip install praisonai, python -m praisonai, or import praisonai statements in Python execution. Combine with Flask/werkzeug imports to identify vulnerable stack assembly.

suggestion.title: Flask 0.0.0.0 Bind Detection (Insecure Configuration)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'binds to 0.0.0.0 per the recommended sample YAML'. UC_9_4 hunts inbound to 8005 but doesn't detect the bind configuration itself. A config-file or process-startup audit would catch pre-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt Flask process commandline arguments or startup config files containing 0.0.0.0, host='0.0.0.0', or app.run(host='0.0.0.0'). Focus on Python processes spawned from deploy workflows.

suggestion.title: Generated API Server Code Pattern Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article names the vulnerable code generator: 'praisonai.deploy.api.generate_api_server_code'. This function signature is the vulnerability origin. No UC hunts the output artifact.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for generated Python files containing specific patterns: @app.route('/chat'), @app.route('/agents'), or Flask boilerplate created by the generate_api_server_code function. Watch for new .py files in temp dirs or deployment paths shortly after `praisonai deploy` execution.

suggestion.title: YAML Deployment Config Inspection (Vulnerable Settings)
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'recommended sample YAML' triggers the vulnerability. UC_9_3 hunts the command, but no UC validates the YAML config for insecure port/bind/auth settings before deployment.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect creation or modification of YAML files containing port: 8005, host: 0.0.0.0, or authentication: disabled/false in the context of praisonai deployments. Pair with process execution of `praisonai deploy` within minutes.

suggestion.title: Default Flask Port 8005 Process Ownership Anomaly
suggestion.rationale: UC_9_4 hunts network inbound, but doesn't correlate process ownership. If a non-service account (e.g., user shell, cron, CI/CD pipeline) spawns the Flask listener, it's a configuration anomaly worth flagging ahead of exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate listening processes on 8005 with initiating process account and parent. Flag if initiated by developer accounts, ad-hoc Python shells, or non-service accounts. Expected: service account or deployment automation; suspicious: interactive user, CI/CD agent, or shell session.

suggestion.title: Forged JWT Token Usage — Multiple User Identities from Single Source
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'allowing token forgery for any user when PLATFORM_ENV is unset'. Detection should target successful authentication events presenting different user principals from the same source IP in rapid succession, which indicates token forgery post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for authentication success events (HTTP 200 on /auth/me or /workspaces/ endpoints) from a single IP address where the authenticated User/Principal changes multiple times within a short window (e.g., 5+ distinct users in 10 minutes). Token forgery bypasses normal session management; rapid user-switching is the fingerprint.

suggestion.title: Hardcoded JWT Secret Detection — Process or Environment Exposure
suggestion.rationale: Article describes: 'JWT signing secret defaults to the hardcoded literal "dev-secret-change-me"'. Forensic detection should flag any process, config file, or log output containing the known hardcoded secret, which would confirm exploitation or misconfiguration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for string 'dev-secret-change-me' or 'dev-secret-change' in process command lines, environment variable dumps, configuration files (*.env, *.json, *.yaml in /etc/praisonai* or app directories), and memory dumps. Any match indicates either a vulnerable default deployment or an attacker who extracted the secret.

suggestion.title: PLATFORM_ENV Environment Exploitation — Absence or Explicit 'dev' Override
suggestion.rationale: Article core flaw: 'A safety check exists but only fires when PLATFORM_ENV != "dev"; the default value of PLATFORM_ENV is "dev"'. Detection should hunt for deployments or runtime invocations where PLATFORM_ENV is explicitly set to 'dev' in production network segments, or missing entirely on production-labeled hosts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for praisonai_platform processes on production/staging-classified hosts where PLATFORM_ENV env var is either absent (relying on dangerous default) or explicitly set to 'dev'. Cross-reference process owner and network location; mismatches (prod network, dev config) indicate misconfiguration or intentional exploitation.

suggestion.title: JWT Token Validation Bypass — Failed auth followed by API success
suggestion.rationale: Article impact: 'allowing token forgery for any user when PLATFORM_ENV is unset'. If attackers craft tokens directly, they may bypass initial auth checks but succeed at API endpoints. Detect HTTP 401→403 (auth fail/forbidden) followed immediately by HTTP 200 (success) on /workspaces or /auth/me with identical or suspicious token signatures.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate HTTP response codes: a source making requests that receive 401 (Unauthorized) or 403 (Forbidden), then immediately switching to 200 OK responses on the same API endpoints without a re-authentication event, suggests token forgery or validation bypass in progress.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Workspace role escalation via API audit logs (successful role-change in application logs)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states the vulnerability is in the `PATCH /workspaces/{workspace_id}/members/{user_id}` endpoint. Application-layer audit logs will show the role-change event. Detection pipeline did not suggest hunting application audit logs at all, only network/endpoint layers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor application audit logs for workspace member role changes (especially escalations to 'owner' or 'admin'). Correlate with originating user_id and timestamp. Flag role changes initiated by non-owner accounts or by accounts that did not previously have admin rights in the workspace.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Access to data endpoints immediately following unauthorized role escalation
suggestion.rationale: After escalating privileges, an attacker would enumerate workspace data they now have access to. Article mentions T1213/T1530 as consequences. No UC detects the data-access phase post-exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After detecting a successful role-escalation PATCH (200/204 response), monitor for GET requests to workspace data endpoints from the same user within 5–30 minutes. Flag if the user accesses resources they could not access before the role change (infer from historical baseline).

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Authorization check bypass — 403 escalation to 200 on member-update endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article states the endpoint is gated by `require_workspace_member(workspace_id)` with `min_role='member'`, never overridden. A sophisticated attacker might first attempt the request and receive 403/401, then escalate. No UC detects this pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for a sequence: HTTP 403/401 response on PATCH /workspaces/*/members/* followed by a 200/204 response on the same endpoint from the same source IP and user within 60 seconds. This suggests reconnaissance followed by successful exploitation.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Bulk workspace member role changes by a single user in short time window
suggestion.rationale: Attack might involve promoting multiple accounts (confederates) to owner in rapid succession. No UC detects bulk role-change activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for a single user initiating PATCH requests to modify member roles on 3+ distinct user_ids within 10 minutes. Flag especially if targeted users are escalated to owner/admin role.

suggestion.title: praisonai-platform: Workspace member role escalation + immediate deactivation of legitimate admin
suggestion.rationale: A more sophisticated attack flow: attacker promotes self, then removes or demotes the legitimate workspace owner to disable recovery. This is a variation of UC_4_3 but framed as disable-owner rather than just demotion.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect a sequence: PATCH request that escalates one user to owner, followed within 30 minutes by a PATCH request that demotes or deactivates a different user who was previously an owner (check baseline). Flag if the first PATCH user and the demoted user differ.

suggestion.title: AI Coding Tool Configuration Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes GitHub Copilot integration and Snyk scanning as critical security controls: 'developers could generate code, receive security findings immediately.' Compromise of these integrations would bypass core controls. No existing detection assumes threat actor targeting AI tool configs themselves.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unauthorized changes to GitHub Copilot settings, Snyk integration auth tokens, or pre-commit hook scripts. Detect lateral movement into developer machine CI/CD tool configs. Alert on revocation/reinstall of security scanning tools by non-admin users.

suggestion.title: Malicious Dependency Injection via AI Output
suggestion.rationale: Article describes AI-generated code flowing directly into commits via custom pre-commit hooks: 'developers could generate code...and apply fixes in real time before code was ever committed.' If AI tool or its supply chain is compromised, malicious dependencies bypass human review.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect novel or typosquatted dependencies introduced in commits that pass pre-commit scanning. Alert on dependencies added by junior developers at unusual times. Correlate with known compromise of popular packages; monitor for duplicate or near-identical dependency names.

suggestion.title: Pre-Commit Hook Bypass or Tampering
suggestion.rationale: Article highlights custom pre-commit hooks as a core security control: 'forces the research right there while it's in front of you.' Attackers with repo access would disable or modify hooks to skip scanning. No detection for hook deletion/modification.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .git/hooks directory for unauthorized deletions, permission changes, or overwrite. Alert on commits that disable or uninstall security scanning tools. Detect when pre-commit output is suppressed or logs are deleted.

suggestion.title: Exfiltration via AI Tool Logs or Generated Code
suggestion.rationale: Article notes developers use AI tools within GitHub for code generation: 'GitHub Copilot matured, Brendan saw a clear shift. Today, AI has become a core part.' AI tools may log sensitive context or generated code to external services; compromise could exfiltrate proprietary algorithms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor network traffic from developer machines to non-standard GitHub or Copilot endpoints. Alert on unusual volumes of data to Microsoft/GitHub services during off-hours. Detect if .copilot config or API keys are read by unexpected processes.

suggestion.title: LinkedIn Spearphishing Link Click Followed by macOS Process Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly describes 'LinkedIn Social Engineering to Deploy Custom macOS Malware.' Pipeline generated zero initial-access or execution detections despite clear phishing vector and payload deployment pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: User clicks malicious link from LinkedIn message or profile, downloads executable disguised as innocuous file. Subsequent process execution from ~/Downloads or /tmp with suspicious command-line arguments (script interpreters, reverse shells, package installation). Look for Python/Bash execution spawned by browser or Archive Utility within 2 minutes of suspicious network activity.

suggestion.title: Suspicious macOS Application Execution from Atypical Paths
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'custom macOS malware' but pipeline captured no execution indicators. Malware deployed via social engineering typically executes from user-writable directories or masquerades as legitimate app.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for executable or script execution from ~/Downloads, ~/Desktop, /tmp, or /var/tmp on macOS. Flag processes spawning child processes with network connectivity (curl, nc, python -m socket) within seconds of user interaction. Custom malware often lacks valid code signatures.

suggestion.title: LinkedIn Profile Reconnaissance for Targeting
suggestion.rationale: Social engineering attack presupposes reconnaissance. Article states actor uses LinkedIn as vector but pipeline captured no discovery/reconnaissance indicators despite this being prerequisite to phishing success.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate LinkedIn API calls or web requests to LinkedIn profile pages of security/sysadmin personnel with subsequent phishing delivery. Profile view patterns (many views from single IP over short window) followed by connection requests and message delivery may signal coordinated social engineering campaign.

suggestion.title: VS Code Tunnels Abuse for C2
suggestion.rationale: Article title states Kimsuky 'Expands Arsenal with VS Code Tunnels'—direct indication of malicious tunnel infrastructure abuse for command and control that pipeline did not surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for VS Code Tunnel daemon processes establishing persistent outbound connections, tunnel ID registration to external relay servers, and VS Code spawning child processes with network-forwarding arguments. Alert on tunnel process creation by non-developer accounts.

suggestion.title: HelloDoor Malware Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title lists 'HelloDoor' as part of Kimsuky's expanded toolkit; pipeline did not propose any detection coverage for this malware family.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HelloDoor process name/hash execution, PowerShell script block logs containing HelloDoor-related download-and-execute patterns, and file system artifacts matching HelloDoor staging directories or installer filenames.

suggestion.title: HTTPSpy HTTPS Exfiltration Detection
suggestion.rationale: Title names HTTPSpy as newly deployed capability; pipeline omitted detection for this tool's HTTPS data exfiltration and reconnaissance command retrieval patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTPS traffic with HTTPSpy user-agent signatures or atypical HTTPS POST patterns to known/suspected Kimsuky C2 infrastructure. Monitor for encrypted tunnel traffic with anomalous byte patterns or timing indicative of exfiltration over HTTP/HTTPS.

suggestion.title: Kimsuky Lateral Movement via Tunnel Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates toolkit expansion for offensive capability; pipeline failed to propose detection for lateral movement abuse of the new tunneling tools.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for repeated tunnel endpoint connections between internal systems, unusual RDP or SSH proxying through VS Code Tunnel relay infrastructure, and lateral movement attempting to establish new tunnel listeners on compromised hosts.

suggestion.title: Kimsuky Malware Family Hash/Signature Coverage
suggestion.rationale: Actor name 'Kimsuky' appears in title but pipeline did not map to known Kimsuky-attributed file hashes, YARA signatures, or TTPs (e.g., WMI execution, scheduled task abuse).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference executable hashes and domains against Kimsuky malware repositories. Alert on Kimsuky-attributed TTPs: WMI command-line execution, scheduled task creation for persistence, and registry modifications matching known Kimsuky malware families.

suggestion.title: Suspicious NuGet Package Installation from Public Repository
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly describes 'malicious NuGet package.' Pipeline missed initial-access vector—likely typosquatting or dependency-confusion attack on legitimate Sicoob SDK.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor nuget.exe and dotnet CLI restore/install activity for fetches of packages matching known SDKs with name variants or unusual source configurations. Alert on installation of packages with similar names to legitimate banking/fintech libraries (typosquatting indicators). Baseline legitimate SDK versions and flag any deviation from pinned versions in internal projects.

suggestion.title: Credential Exfiltration from Banking Software Context
suggestion.rationale: Article states malware 'exfiltrates banking passwords'; pipeline missed credential-access and exfiltration detections. Attack specifically targets Sicoob integration layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect LSASS access, credential store enumeration (CredEnumerate, CredRead Win32 API), or registry queries for banking software config/password storage from .NET runtime processes. Alert on process chains where NuGet or dependency resolution precedes credential-dumping activity by <1 hour. Monitor for in-memory credential extraction patterns via .NET reflection or P/Invoke.

suggestion.title: .NET Assembly Execution from Package Cache with Malicious Behavior
suggestion.rationale: Malicious code embedded in NuGet package executes during dependency resolution or assembly load. Pipeline missed execution-phase detection specific to .NET supply-chain attacks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for child processes or unsigned assembly loads originating from NuGet cache directory (%USERPROFILE%\.nuget\packages). Flag .NET compiler/runtime processes (csc.exe, dotnet.exe, msbuild.exe) spawning unexpected child processes. Correlate assembly load events with subsequent network connections or file writes to credential paths.

suggestion.title: C2 Communication from .NET Process with Exfiltrated Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Article describes password exfiltration; pipeline missed exfiltration-phase detection. Malware communicates with attacker infrastructure to transmit stolen banking credentials.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound TLS connections from .NET runtime processes to non-whitelisted destinations (especially non-banking infrastructure). Alert on POST/PUT traffic from .NET processes carrying base64-encoded or compressed payloads (credential blobs). Correlate credential-access event timestamps with outbound network connections within 5-minute window.

suggestion.title: Anomalous NuGet Source Configuration or Repository Access
suggestion.rationale: Supply-chain attack may involve malicious NuGet source added to project or substitution of legitimate source. Pipeline did not capture repo-level attack detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor changes to NuGet.Config files (additions of non-standard sources, source reordering). Alert on restore operations against internal/private feeds followed by installation from external feeds (priority inversion). Flag projects with 'Allow Prerelease' or disabled signature verification settings.

suggestion.title: Persistence via Malicious NuGet Dependency in Project File
suggestion.rationale: Article indicates SDK replacement; attackers typically persist through project dependencies to re-infect on rebuild. Pipeline missed persistence-phase detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor .csproj, .fsproj, .vbproj files for package references to suspicious package names or versions. Alert on package version downgrades or switches to less-stable versions (pre-release tags). Track projects that depend on packages with high edit/upload frequency (possible attacker re-uploads after deletion/restoration).

suggestion.title: Malicious NuGet/npm Package Installation with Credential Access
suggestion.rationale: Article core claim: 'Malicious Sicoob NuGet Steals Banking Credentials' — packages must be detected during installation, then correlated with subsequent credential-system access (Windows Credential Manager, SAM, cloud credential files).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate NuGet.exe or npm.exe process execution with child processes accessing credential stores (Windows Credential Manager registry hives, .aws/credentials, ~/.azure/*, .gcp/*). Alert on 'Sicoob' or known-malicious package installation followed by Credential Manager enumeration or cloud CLI credential reads.

suggestion.title: Cloud Secret Enumeration and Exfiltration from Package Execution Context

suggestion.rationale: Article describes the patch bypass allowing access to blocked modules; exploitation requires code executing within the vm2 context to access require('child_process') or similar. No hunt detects actual exploitation code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor vm2 runtime errors/warnings or application logs for attempts to access restricted modules from within sandboxed code. Look for patterns like 'require is not defined' followed by module escaping attempts, or successful imports of child_process, fs, os from within vm2 context. Correlate with Node.js parent process event.

suggestion.title: vm2 package.json version inventory filtered to CVE-2026-47137 vulnerable range (≤3.11.3)
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability exists in vm2 ≤3.11.3. UC_20_3 detects presence but not version. Asset inventory must be scoped to vulnerable versions only to be actionable.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Parse package.json version field in all node_modules/vm2 instances. Filter to versions ≤3.11.3. Prioritize internet-facing Node.js applications (web frameworks, API servers, LLM execution environments). Cross-reference with running process tree to identify which hosts have vulnerable vm2 loaded in active process memory.

suggestion.title: LLM integration or code-execution-as-a-service pattern with vm2 deployment—attack surface proxy
suggestion.rationale: Article title emphasizes 'nesting:true' which is a vm2 setting used in LLM sandboxing contexts (allowing nested VM calls). Most exploitation risk is in web-facing LLM services; attacks likely target these. Generic vm2 detection misses context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify Node.js applications that are (1) internet-facing (listening on 0.0.0.0 or public IP, port 80/443/3000/5000), (2) running with vm2 module loaded, and (3) receiving inbound HTTP POST/GET requests to code-execution or 'eval' endpoints. Combine with process spawn behavior (UC_20_2) to detect exploitation attempts against these services specifically.

suggestion.title: CVE-2023-37903 fix bypass indicators—options.require type confusion (undefined vs false)
suggestion.rationale: Article root cause: 'check uses strict equality (options.require === false)' but attacker omits require option entirely, making it undefined. Detection should look for code patterns exploiting this type confusion or code review of vulnerable instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan application code for vm2/NodeVM instantiation where the require option is not explicitly specified. Flag cases where nesting:true is set but require is missing (not set to false). Code review tool integration: report lines where NodeVM constructor is called with nesting but missing require parameter.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-47140 vulnerable vm2 inventory — denylist bypass surface detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'NodeVM blocks several dangerous Node.js builtins...However, the denylist misses process and inspector/promises'. Explicit IOC 'CVE-2026-47140' under Indicators section. UC_18_2 in article shows this hunt maps to 'weapon' phase with high confidence. Pipeline generated zero IOCs or version-match detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for npm/vm2 package with SoftwareVersion matching regex ^3.(?:[0-9]|10|11.[0-3])(?:\.|$) or direct CVE-2026-47140 flag in vulnerability scans. Prioritize internet-facing systems running Node.js application stacks.

suggestion.title: NodeVM denylist bypass PoC keyword hunt — getBuiltinModule and inspector/promises access
suggestion.rationale: Article directly states attack mechanism: 'Both [process and inspector/promises] can be used from sandboxed code to reach host-side execution primitives.' UC_18_4 identifies concrete bypass patterns: 'getBuiltinModule', 'inspector/promises', 'Runtime.evaluate', 'require(\'process\').getBuiltinModule'. These are attack-specific IOC-like strings Pipeline completely missed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for process command lines or code files (.js, .mjs, .cjs) containing bypass pattern strings when executed or created by Node.js process. Alert if these patterns appear outside legitimate npm/yarn/pnpm package manager contexts.

suggestion.title: Node.js spawning native shell interpreter post-denylist escape
suggestion.rationale: Article describes impact: 'allows sandboxed code to bypass the intended builtin restrictions and execute code in the host process.' UC_18_3 targets post-exploit behavior—Node.js parent spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, wmic, etc. Pipeline generated zero impact-phase detections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation where InitiatingProcessFileName matches 'node.exe' or 'node' and child FileName is native shell interpreter (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, bash, sh, wmic.exe, etc.) spawned by non-system account. Reduce FP by excluding npm/yarn/pnpm cache/bin directories.

suggestion.title: Sandboxed code module enumeration — process.getBuiltinModule access patterns
suggestion.rationale: Article core attack: 'The denylist misses process and inspector/promises.' T1480 (Execution Guardrails) maps to circumventing sandbox restrictions. Detection should target attempts to enumerate or access forbidden builtin modules that bypass the NodeVM denylist.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Node.js process for calls to require('process').getBuiltinModule(), require('inspector/promises'), or direct module.builtinModules enumeration when running under sandboxed/isolated context. Alert on access patterns that bypass documented NodeVM restrictions.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable NodeVM/vm2 application deployment in production
suggestion.rationale: Article vulnerability: CVE-2026-47140 affects deployed applications using vm2 ≤3.11.3 for code sandboxing. T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application) applies. Detection should identify running applications with vulnerable dependencies before exploitation occurs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Asset discovery hunt: identify Node.js applications with package.json or package-lock.json dependencies on vm2 with vulnerable version range. Cross-reference with Shodan/internet-facing assets. Alert on applications accepting user-controlled script input to sandboxed vm2 context.

suggestion.title: vm2 Promise.prototype constructor manipulation – runtime behavior
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'localPromise constructor... calling this.then(undefined, eater)... missing a call to resetPromiseSpecies to ensure that this has no special species.' UC_21_3 only fingerprints PoC source strings; none monitor the actual Promise constructor chain manipulation (Symbol.species binding, .then() chaining) during sandbox execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor node.exe for Symbol.species getters/setters on Promise.prototype, custom .then() implementations that circumvent resetPromiseSpecies, or constructor property access chains that precede child_process spawning by <5 seconds.

suggestion.title: Code injection into vm2 sandbox – initial access & delivery
suggestion.rationale: Article describes vulnerable vm2 accepting attacker code ('attackers to write code which can escape from the VM2 sandbox') but no UC hunts how that code reaches the vm2 instance. Missing detection for vm2 code loading from untrusted sources, script injection via API, or file-based code drops preceding execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect node.exe or npm.exe processes loading or executing .js/.mjs files immediately before spawn of child processes, especially when sources are user-controlled (web uploads, API request bodies, temp files).

suggestion.title: WebAssembly JSPI API invocation from untrusted code context
