Detect Flutter processes spawning shells (/bin/bash, /bin/zsh) or invoking system utilities suggestive of post-exploitation activity.

suggestion.title: macOS Login Item Persistence—Backdoor Survival Mechanism
suggestion.rationale: Backdoor sustainability requires persistence. Article establishes 'FlutterShell backdoor' maintains access, but zero UCs address T1547.001 (Login Items) registration typical of macOS malware.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor creation/modification of plist files in ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and /Library/LaunchDaemons/ that reference Flutter binaries, unsigned executables, or shell wrappers. Correlate timestamps with recent malware execution or suspicious downloads.

suggestion.title: FlutterShell C2 Beaconing—Novel Backdoor Command Channel
suggestion.rationale: Backdoor operation assumes C2 communication. Article identifies 'new FlutterShell backdoor'—infrastructure is novel and IOCs unavailable to pipeline. No UC addresses behavioral detection of C2 polling from Flutter processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag macOS processes with executable source paths from user Downloads/Temp initiating outbound HTTPS to newly-registered or low-reputation domains (reputation age <60 days). Alert on periodic connection attempts (15m–1h intervals) to the same destination.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Executable Download from Ad-Network Origin
suggestion.rationale: Malvertising payload delivery is the infection point: 'distributed the new backdoor FlutterShell.' No UC detects files downloaded from ad-network CDNs or tracking-pixel domains arriving as executable code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on file downloads from known ad-exchange, affiliate, or ad-tech domains (.ads, tracking subdomains, ad.cdn) landing as Mach-O binaries or disk images in user-writable locations. Correlate user browsing history with download metadata.

suggestion.title: Malicious Minecraft JAR file execution from game directories
suggestion.rationale: Article states '3,820 unique malicious JAR files' and distribution 'through Minecraft-related malicious mods, clients, cheats, and utilities.' Pipeline extracted zero use cases despite explicit JAR-based execution mechanism being the delivery vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of .JAR files from Minecraft application directories (AppData/Roaming/.minecraft/mods or equivalent). Correlate with suspicious parent processes or network connections to known malicious domains. High-risk if JAR sourced from domains other than official Minecraft Launcher or certified mod repositories.

suggestion.title: Browser credential and session store access by suspicious processes
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly lists infostealer targets: 'Minecraft session ID theft, cookies, and saved passwords across 36 browsers, 56 cryptocurrency add-ons...Discord, Steam, and Telegram credentials.' No detection use cases were generated for this core attack activity.

Alert on unusual file access or registry reads targeting Session/Cookie storage by non-browser processes. Baseline and flag processes executing from game mod directories.

suggestion.title: SEO poisoning and domain spoofing of legitimate Minecraft mod projects
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'SEO poisoning distribution method targets keywords corresponding to clients: Meteor Client, Radium Client, Wurst Client, Aristois, LiquidBounce, Impact Client...' and highlights fake site for 'Skytils' linking to legitimate GitHub to build trust. Zero IOCs or detections for this domain-spoofing attack vector.

Monitor for domains hosting .JAR files with names matching real projects but originating from untrusted registrars. Cross-reference against legitimate GitHub and Discord repositories for mod projects.

suggestion.title: YouTube-facilitated malware distribution via description and comment links
suggestion.rationale: Article states WeedHack 'reaches victims mainly through YouTube videos showcasing Minecraft-related tools...attacker drops download links in descriptions and comments.' Some videos accumulated 7,500+ views. Pipeline generated zero detections for this distribution channel.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound network traffic from endpoints for clicks or downloads from YouTube video description links and user comments. Correlate YouTube engagement with subsequent downloads of .JAR or suspicious executables. Alert on traffic patterns consistent with malware-distribution campaigns (many users accessing same malicious domain after viewing same YouTube channel).

suggestion.title: Remote access tool indicators: unexpected webcam, keyboard, and mouse access
suggestion.rationale: Article describes premium WeedHack tier ($5/month or $24.99 lifetime) offers 'remote control with input access (mouse and keyboard), webcam access, keylogger, remote shell, and remote file management.' Zero detection use cases for this capability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on unexpected process access to webcam/microphone APIs from non-standard applications, particularly those with Minecraft or gaming-context in their path or parent process. Monitor for unusual input simulation events (mouse/keyboard events from non-input devices). Baseline webcam access and flag anomalies from game mod processes.

suggestion.title: WeedHack dashboard and Telegram C2 communication indicators
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'WeedHack platform hosted on the clear net' with a 'Telegram channel' having '800+ members.' These are direct C2 indicators. Pipeline extracted zero IOCs for the C2 infrastructure or communication channels.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for network traffic to known WeedHack C2 domain/IP (requires OSINT to identify). Flag Telegram API calls originating from Minecraft mod processes or suspicious executables in game directories. Alert on exfiltration of credential data to untrusted C2 endpoints.

suggestion.title: Xeno RAT Process and Behavioral Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly names 'Xeno RAT' as delivery/persistence payload in targeted attack against government finance ministry. No execution-phase or C2 detection use cases generated despite RAT being the core technical indicator.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Xeno RAT typically executes via PowerShell or WScript with network beaconing to C2. Monitor for unsigned PowerShell processes spawning suspicious network outbound connections, registry modifications to persistence paths (Run, RunOnce keys), or process hollowing patterns indicative of RAT deployment.

suggestion.title: SideCopy Phishing Campaign Against Afghan Finance Ministry
suggestion.rationale: Title identifies targeted attack on 'Afghanistan Finance Ministry' by 'Pakistan-linked SideCopy' but pipeline produced no initial-access or credential-access detections. Phishing is standard SideCopy TTP for government targeting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for emails sent to Afghanistan Finance Ministry domains with embedded Office documents or archive attachments; cross-reference sender domains against known SideCopy campaign infrastructure. Flag suspicious URL clicks from targeted users leading to credential-harvesting pages or malware downloader sites.

suggestion.title: SideCopy Actor Identification and Attribution
suggestion.rationale: Title contains explicit actor attribution ('Pakistan-linked SideCopy') but pipeline failed to surface threat actor name, country nexus, or historical campaign patterns. Actor names are foundational for alert enrichment and threat hunting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate against known SideCopy C2 infrastructure (if disclosed in article). SideCopy typically uses HTTP/HTTPS for RAT C2 with possible domain-fronting or proxy chains. Monitor for outbound connections from Afghanistan Finance Ministry systems to Pakistani IP ranges or previously-attributed C2 domains.

suggestion.title: Malicious Java Dependency Version in Build Manifest
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'Package: net.jqwik:jqwik-engine, Affected version: 1.10.0, Follow-up release: 1.10.1'. Direct supply chain IOC.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag any pom.xml, build.gradle, or Maven resolution log containing net.jqwik:jqwik-engine version 1.10.0. Cross-reference transitively pulled versions in lock files. Alert on any Java project in agent-integrated environments (Claude Code, Copilot agent mode, Cursor) that includes this version.

suggestion.title: ANSI Terminal Escape Sequences in CI/CD and Agent-Visible Output
suggestion.rationale: Article describes core evasion: 'prints ESC[2K followed by a carriage return, twice... invisible to a human watching a terminal. But on any stream that records output as raw text, those erase codes are just dead characters. The instruction stays right there in the log.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on raw ANSI control sequences (0x1B[2K, CR sequences) appearing in CI/CD logs, IDE test output panels, or agent-consumed streams, especially clustering near suspicious text. Flag as potential attempt to hide malicious content from human eyes while leaving it intact for machine parsers.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Agent-Targeting Method Names in Decompiled Dependencies
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'The malicious instruction lived in a new method called printMessageForCodingAgents()... The method name tells you the intent on its own.' Explicitly marked method for AI agent interaction.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan decompiled JARs and published source code for method/function names explicitly referencing 'agent', 'LLM', 'AI', 'agentic', or 'coding_agent'. Flag unusual console-output methods with agent-targeting names as potential prompt injection vectors, especially in testing or execution frameworks.

suggestion.title: Prompt Injection Payloads in Test Framework Output Fed to AI Agents
suggestion.rationale: Article core threat model: 'Agentic coding tools fold terminal and test output back into their context while they work. So a destructive line buried in that output can get read as a real command... The payload told agents to disregard previous instructions and delete all jqwik tests and code.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor streams piped into AI coding agents for injection-style payloads with imperatives ('delete', 'disregard previous instructions', 'override'), especially originating from test framework output (JUnit, Gradle, Maven). Flag as attempted prompt injection if instructions conflict with normal agent workflow.

suggestion.title: Supply Chain Protestware: Intentional Sabotage by Package Maintainer
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes: 'the maintainer of jqwik... released version 1.10.0... with a hidden instruction... It was intentional... Not an outside attacker who hijacked the account... Johannes Link, the project's own maintainer.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor package release notes and maintainer statements for admissions of intentional injection, ideological objections to AI agent use, or cryptic behavior changes. Cross-reference recent maintainer public statements about refusing to support agentic coding tools. Flag maintainer-intentional sabotage separately from compromise-based supply chain attacks.

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Package Install Script Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article references 'wormable malware' and 'multi-stage attacks'; npm postinstall scripts are the delivery vector for supply-chain payloads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm install / npx execution in CI/CD environments, especially when followed by unsigned or obfuscated child processes (curl, sh, powershell). Alert on scripts that spawn network utilities (curl, wget, nc) or credential-access tools (history, env, git config) immediately after package installation.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting from npm/GitHub Environment Variables
suggestion.rationale: Article keywords include 'Credential Harvesting'; supply-chain attacks in npm commonly steal NPM_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN from CI/CD build containers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag processes (node, npm, install scripts) that read .npmrc, invoke 'env', 'printenv', 'cat ~/.ssh/config', or git credential-osxkeychain within npm install context. Correlate with outbound HTTPS connections to non-standard npm registries or attacker-controlled domains.

suggestion.title: Worm-like Dependency Injection in package.json
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'worm propagation'; npm worms modify package.json to inject themselves into dependent projects.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unsigned or untrusted package.json modifications that add new dependencies pointing to internal or typosquatted npm packages immediately after npm install. Correlate with commit activity from CI/CD service accounts or unexpected branch commits.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated Code Patterns in npm Package Artifacts
suggestion.rationale: Article keywords include 'obfuscation' and 'payload'; malicious npm packages often use minification, base64, or IIFE patterns to evade detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Scan downloaded npm packages (in node_modules) for base64-encoded strings, hex-encoded payloads, or eval() calls in non-development dependencies. Flag packages with suspicious comment density and class/variable names that don't match declared functionality.

suggestion.title: Anomalous npm Registry Authentication and Package Publish
suggestion.rationale: Article is about npm supply chain; attackers publish malicious packages using compromised or typosquatted accounts. Monitor registry login and publish activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag npm publish commands from unusual geolocations, IP addresses, or times relative to account baseline. Alert on package versions published with version bumps that skip semver semantics or contain pre-release/build metadata without corresponding source control tags.

suggestion.title: Suspicious HTTP Requests to Steam Community Profile Pages from Internal Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states attackers hide 'command instructions inside Steam Community profile comments'. Malware must fetch and parse comments from specific profile URLs. Detection: internal/private hosts making repeated requests to steamcommunity.com/profiles/* or steamcommunity.com/id/* endpoints with short intervals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for processes (especially PHP-based or web-server contexts) initiating outbound HTTPS to steamcommunity.com with targeted profile or ID paths. Flag requests originating from known WordPress-hosting infrastructure, especially with high request frequency, off-hours access, or specific profile ID repetition suggesting polling.

suggestion.title: WordPress Process Executing Commands Derived from Fetched Web Content
suggestion.rationale: Core attack mechanism: malware fetches comments (unstructured web content) and executes embedded commands. Article states 'hiding command instructions inside Steam Community profile comments'. Detection: PHP or WordPress processes fetching remote HTML/JSON, parsing, and executing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate outbound HTTPS requests to Steam or malware domains with subsequent process creation (e.g., cmd.exe, bash, powershell spawned from PHP/apache) within 1-5 seconds. Flag PHP functions like eval(), exec(), system(), passthru() called after remote content fetch. Look for obfuscated or base64-encoded arguments.

suggestion.title: Injected or Modified WordPress Plugin/Theme Code Loading External Commands
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'malware campaign targeting WordPress websites'. Malware persistence requires injection into WordPress plugin, theme, or core files. Detection: suspicious PHP code in wp-content/plugins, wp-content/themes, or wp-admin with eval/exec/curl operations and external domain references.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WordPress directories for newly created or modified PHP files containing high-entropy strings, base64 blocks, or known malware signatures. Flag write operations from non-standard accounts (web-server user writing outside expected paths). Detect PHP process loading these files followed by network connections to attacker infrastructure.

suggestion.title: WordPress Database Write Operations with Suspicious Encoded Content
suggestion.rationale: Malware must persist across requests. WordPress stores data in wp_posts, wp_postmeta, wp_options. Article describes 'malware campaign' implying persistent installation. Detection: database INSERTs/UPDATEs with high-entropy or base64-encoded payloads in text fields.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WordPress database for INSERT/UPDATE operations on wp_posts.post_content, wp_postmeta.meta_value, wp_options.option_value containing obfuscated or base64 PHP code, or references to external domains (especially hello-mywordl.info). Correlate with file-system changes in wp-content/plugins/uploads directories.

suggestion.title: Outbound Connections from Web-Server User to Attacker-Controlled Domains
suggestion.rationale: IOC 'hello-mywordl.info' suggests malware downloads payload or receives supplementary commands from this domain. Article doesn't detail role, but WordPress malware typically beacons to attacker infrastructure.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag any network connection from web-server process (apache, nginx, httpd, www-data user) to hello-mywordl.info or other IOCs in article. Elevated alert if connection occurs during off-hours, uses non-standard ports, or is followed by file/process modifications in WordPress directories.

suggestion.title: Unauthenticated Access to Plaintext Credential Log (CVE-2026-49200)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'acer_cgi.log file...accessible without authentication via the web interface' and 'contains cleartext login credentials (for web and Telnet)'—direct, trivial credential exposure vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unauthenticated HTTP requests to acer_cgi.log or /admin paths on Acer Wave 7 routers. Alert on successful (200) responses to log requests without valid session/auth tokens. Correlate extracted credentials with subsequent Telnet or SSH login attempts from same or different source.

suggestion.title: Hardcoded AES Key Backup Decryption and Modification (CVE-2026-49201)
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'upload.cgi binary...contains a hardcoded AES encryption key' permitting attackers to 'decrypt, modify, and re-encrypt system backups, facilitating persistent backdoor injection'—core persistence mechanism.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor upload.cgi invocation patterns; flag backup file access followed by decryption operations using publicly-disclosed hardcoded keys. Detect file modifications within backup archives post-decryption. Alert on firmware restore operations that introduce unexpected binaries or autostart entries.

suggestion.title: Telnet Remote Code Execution via Leaked Router Credentials
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies plaintext Telnet credentials stored in acer_cgi.log as attack surface, enabling remote command execution on compromised routers.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate credentials extracted from Acer router logs with Telnet authentication attempts on the same or related infrastructure. Alert on successful Telnet logins using credentials matching router credential file format. Track shell command execution post-Telnet authentication.

suggestion.title: Remote Admin Interface Access from Untrusted Sources
suggestion.rationale: Article recommends disabling remote management and restricting 'Internet remote access to trusted IP addresses'—indicates remote web console (http://192.168.76.1, acerconnect.com) is primary exploitation entry point for both CVEs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP/HTTPS access to Acer Wave 7 admin interfaces from non-local subnets or external IP ranges. Alert on geo-anomalies (access from countries outside operational footprint). Track failed login attempts followed by successful credential-less access (CVE-2026-49200 exploitation).

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Acer Wave 7 Firmware Version Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies firmware version 'T7c_GBL_1.01.000055 or earlier' are vulnerable; asset inventory and patch tracking critical for risk remediation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query or scan Acer Wave 7 routers for firmware version; flag any <= T7c_GBL_1.01.000055. Maintain inventory of vulnerable devices. Monitor for firmware update attempts and validate successful patch deployment to versions > T7c_GBL_1.01.000055.

suggestion.title: Post-Restoration Backdoor Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article describes hardcoded-key attack enabling 'persistent backdoor injection' via modified backups—post-compromise forensics indicator requiring process and network baseline deviations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected process spawning within minutes of backup restore operations. Detect new cron/autostart entries in restored configurations. Alert on network traffic deviations (outbound connections, C2 signatures) following firmware restore on Acer routers.

suggestion.title: DLL Side-Loading via Hentai Game Distribution (FFmpeg Hijacking)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes modified FFmpeg DLL importing from natives2_blob.bin: 'modified FFmpeg DLL...imported DllGetClassObject from a file called natives2_blob.bin...the library loads as soon as the user starts the game.' Clear execution vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect ffmpeg.dll loads from non-system paths (game directories). Monitor for unusual DLL imports or parent processes launching PowerShell post-load. Establish baseline for legitimate game ffmpeg behavior.

suggestion.title: COM Registry InprocServer32 Hijacking for Persistence
suggestion.rationale: Article states persistence mechanism: 'COM hijacking to persist on the victim's machine, replacing the InprocServer32 entry for Windows Color System Calibration Loader DLL...triggered when the user logs in.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on modifications to InprocServer32 values under CLSID registry keys, especially entries pointing to non-standard system paths. Monitor registry writes from game process parents or unusual callers with startup trigger timing.

suggestion.title: Base64-Encoded PowerShell Execution from Game DLL
suggestion.rationale: Article describes Stage1 loader: 'natives2_blob.bin file is a DLL that executes a Base64-encoded PowerShell script when loaded.' Direct indicator of obfuscated code execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect PowerShell invocations with -EncodedCommand or -enc flags spawned from game directories or DLL-loaded parent processes. Decode Base64 payloads in monitoring to surface malicious intent. Correlate with ffmpeg.dll or natives2_blob.bin loads.

suggestion.title: Sandbox/VM Detection Behavior in Game Process
suggestion.rationale: Article notes Stage1 'performs basic checks for controlled environments' before Stage2 download, indicating anti-sandbox/analysis logic.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag PowerShell commands from game processes that enumerate system info via Get-WmiObject, systeminfo, or wmic with VM/hypervisor-detection keywords. Alert on strings referencing Hyper-V, VirtualBox, or debugger detection.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation C2 Communication from Game Process
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'implant downloads and executes a Trojan, resulting in full system compromise and broad remote control capabilities.' C2 beaconing must occur post-sandbox check.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish game-process network baselines; alert on unexpected outbound connections to non-CDN endpoints, especially from processes loaded via DLL hijacking chain. Monitor for sustained C2 communication patterns post-execution.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Artifact Creation in Game Directory
suggestion.rationale: Delivery archive contains 'fully functional, legitimate game files, as well as a modified FFmpeg DLL' and natives2_blob.bin. File creation patterns at game installation are forensic artifacts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor file creation in game installation directories for DLL/BIN files alongside game launch. Flag .bin files or DLLs with suspicious names (natives2_blob.bin). Cross-reference with extraction tool process parents.

suggestion.title: Spear-Phishing with Business Document Disguise (T1566.001)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly: 'disguises itself as an everyday business document — a purchase order, a quote, or a request for proposal.' This is the entry point. Pipeline detected no email-layer hunt.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag emails from external senders with attachments matching PO/quote patterns (file names like *PO*, *Quote*, *RFP*, or *Invoice*) or suspicious script-like extensions (.js, .jse, .vbs, .wsf, .hta). High-signal if recipient is non-procurement user, attachment is zipped, or Office file with OLE2/Active Content. Cross-reference against SMTP logs for sender reputation.

suggestion.title: Document Viewer Spawning Script Interpreter (T1204.002 + T1059.007)
suggestion.rationale: User opens document → malware executes. Article implies this chain; pipeline provided no process-creation detection. Critical execution chokepoint.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect parent-child process chain: (winword.exe | excel.exe | AcroRd32.exe | powerpnt.exe | explorer.exe) spawning (cscript.exe | wscript.exe | node.exe | powershell.exe). Suspicious if child's command line contains -NoProfile, -Encoded, eval(), or Function(); working directory is %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, or Downloads; or spawn time is <5s after parent launch.

suggestion.title: Obfuscated JavaScript Execution via WSH (T1059.007 + T1027)
suggestion.rationale: Malware is 'JS.MonoGlyphRAT'—JavaScript-based RAT. Pipeline identified T1071 but missed T1059.007 entirely. Must detect obfuscation patterns in script execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag cscript.exe or wscript.exe with suspicious command-line indicators: hex-encoded strings (0x41 patterns), Base64 in arguments, string concatenation with ampersand (&), or evidence of eval/Function construction. Also detect .js files executed directly from %TEMP%, %APPDATA%\Local\Temp, or email attachment folder like Outlook cache.

suggestion.title: C2 Beaconing via DNS or HTTP to aryamint.com Subdomains (T1071 + T1568.002)
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline named T1071 but generated no beaconing hunt. Must detect repeated polling/heartbeat traffic to C2 domains, not just single connections.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect high-frequency DNS queries to subdomains of aryamint.com or scan.aryamint.com (e.g., ≥10 queries in 60s) or beaconing pattern: HTTP/HTTPS connections to 158.94.211.76 / 91.92.243.79 at regular intervals (every 30-300s), small payloads (<1KB request/response), or non-standard ports (not 80/443). Correlate source to cscript.exe / document handler process.

suggestion.title: RAT Payload Staging & Persistence (T1105 + T1547.001)
suggestion.rationale: JS RAT must drop additional payloads or establish persistence. Article calls malware 'stealthy'—suggests evasion of writes. No file/registry/task creation hunts provided.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for .js, .exe, .dll, .ps1 files created in %TEMP%, %APPDATA%\Local, user Downloads, or ProgramData within 30s of document open. Watch for registry modifications under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, StartupFolder, or HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU. Flag Task Scheduler event creation with JavaScript execution or cscript.exe scheduled tasks.

suggestion.title: Post-Infection System Enumeration by RAT (T1057 + T1518.001)
suggestion.rationale: RAT tradecraft includes process/software discovery. Article mentions 'stealthy' but does not show evasion pattern—pipeline missed reconnaissance phase entirely. Standard RAT behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect child processes spawned by cscript.exe / wscript.exe executing reconnaissance commands: tasklist, taskmgr, Get-Process, systeminfo, whoami, ipconfig, nslookup, wmic, reg.exe queries to HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet. High-signal if multiple enum commands execute in rapid succession (burst pattern) or parent process is non-interactive.

suggestion.title: Download fake Minecraft client from SEO-poisoned search or YouTube video
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'hackers are hiding dangerous malware inside what look like popular Minecraft mods and game clients, using YouTube videos and search engine tricks to pull unsuspecting players into their trap.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on executable downloads from YouTube CDN, unfamiliar gaming sites, or IP 92.119.164.235 after search-engine or video-hosting referrers with Minecraft keywords. Correlate download timing and filename with known game-distribution patterns.

suggestion.title: User execution of masqueraded Minecraft client matching known hashes
suggestion.rationale: 30 provided SHA256 hashes indicate variant malware disguised as legitimate mod/client software. T1036 (Masquerading) is implicit in 'looks like popular' description.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag process creation from Downloads, Desktop, or AppData\Temp directories matching any of 30 provided hashes or with Minecraft-themed naming (Krypton, Xenon, Odin, Nova, aether). Alert on child processes to network resources within seconds of execution.

suggestion.title: Outbound C2 communication to stealer infrastructure domains
suggestion.rationale: Multiple IOC domains explicitly named 'stealer' (acabstealer.ru, stealer.to, stealer.cy, 1312stealer.ru) and payment/exfil points (whpayment.ru, whnewreceive.ru, whreceiverrrrrrrrr.ru) indicate credential/data theft. 116,000 victims suggests active harvesting.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on DNS resolution or outbound connections to stealer.*, weedhack.*, whpayment.ru, whreceiver*.ru, 92.119.164.235, or other listed domains. Establish persistence by monitoring for recurring communication pattern post-malware execution.

suggestion.title: Credential and data exfiltration via stealer malware
suggestion.rationale: Campaign nomenclature (stealer domains) and victim scale (116,000+) indicate systematic credential/file harvesting. Article body truncated but core functionality is exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for clipboard APIs, screenshot/screen-recording library calls, keylogging patterns, or memory scraping post-malware execution. Alert on credential store access (Windows Credential Manager, browser password stores, Minecraft launcher config files). Correlate internal data access with outbound network events to stealer C2.

suggestion.title: File hash match on WeedHack variant collection
suggestion.rationale: Article provides 30 distinct SHA256 hashes representing known malware variants. Standard IOC-based endpoint detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on file creation or process execution with SHA256 matching any of 30 provided hashes. Supplement with behavioral detonation rules if obfuscation (T1027) defeats static matching.

suggestion.title: YouTube/Discord bot commands triggering malware downloads
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'hackers are hiding dangerous malware inside what look like popular Minecraft mods'. YouTube platform implies video-embedded links or comments; investigate for bot-driven referral chains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP/HTTPS requests with referrer headers from youtube.com, youtu.be, or discord.com to known malware domains or 92.119.164.235. Alert on bulk download patterns from single YouTube video ID suggesting coordinated campaign sourcing.

suggestion.title: Active Directory Enumeration via Net.exe or LDAP
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'Active Directory discovery' using automated AI tools; manifests as anomalous net.exe enumeration (net group, net user) or LDAP query storms.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on rapid sequences of net.exe with enumeration flags or LDAP queries from a single source to domain controllers; correlate with process originating from user-writable paths or spawned by PowerShell/cmd executed from suspicious parent.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Payload Execution from User Directories
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'payloads stored in a user directory' triggered 'suspicious endpoint alerts'—indicates execution from %APPDATA%, Desktop, Downloads.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unsigned child processes or obfuscated script execution originating from %APPDATA%, %USERPROFILE%\Downloads, Desktop; flag if process subsequently modifies registry, creates services, or communicates to external IPs.

suggestion.title: EDR Tool Enumeration and Evasion Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'EDR evasion techniques'—implies WMI queries for antivirus processes, registry inspection of EDR vendor hives, or service termination attempts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect WMI queries with antivirus/EDR filters, registry reads of HKLM\Software\<security vendor>, taskkill or net stop targeting EDR services; flag obfuscated PowerShell/scripts and API hooking indicators (VirtualProtect, SetWindowsHookEx).

suggestion.title: Domain Trust Discovery and Lateral Movement Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Post-exploitation framework context and 'AI-assisted tools' imply automated trust topology and remote system discovery prior to lateral movement.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor execution of nltest.exe /domain_trusts, dsquery, PowerShell Get-AdForest or remote system probing (ping, wmic /node, psexec reconnaissance); correlate with non-administrative user context or cascade from initial compromise endpoint.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Framework Staging and Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article mentions 'structured collection of malicious components forming a post-exploitation framework'—should detect tooling signatures (mimikatz, Impacket, PowerView).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on command-line strings characteristic of post-ex tools (Invoke-Mimikatz, Get-NetComputer, secretsdump.py); monitor for staging in temp directories or file shares followed by remote execution; flag unusual library imports (advapi32, netapi32, samlib).

suggestion.title: HTTP/2 Stream Multiplication Attack Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'HTTP/2 Bomb Vulnerability Allows Remote DoS'; the attack vector involves malformed HTTP/2 frames triggering resource exhaustion. Pipeline missed detection for abnormal stream creation per connection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor single HTTP/2 connections for rapid stream ID creation (>100 streams in <5 seconds) or stream ID wraparound anomalies. Correlate with memory/CPU spikes in web server process.

suggestion.title: HTTP/2 Header Compression Bomb (HPACK Explosion)
suggestion.rationale: HTTP/2 Bomb attacks exploit HPACK to trigger exponential decompression. Article explicitly names vulnerability type but pipeline did not map to compression-based DoS vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on HPACK header decompression size ratios >10,000:1 (e.g., 50 bytes compressed → 500KB decompressed) or total decompressed header size >50MB per connection.

suggestion.title: HTTP/2 RST_STREAM Flood to Induce DoS
suggestion.rationale: Known HTTP/2 DoS vector via rapid RST_STREAM frames. Article lists affected servers (NGINX, Apache, IIS, Envoy, Cloudflare) but pipeline did not identify stream-reset abuse pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect >500 RST_STREAM frames per connection in 60 seconds, or RST_STREAM rate exceeding 10x baseline request-completion rate.

suggestion.title: Web Server Crash Correlated with Malformed HTTP/2 Frames
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'Allows Remote DoS on NGINX, Apache, IIS, Envoy & Cloudflare'; implies crash/unavailability. Pipeline did not generate use case linking server logs to HTTP/2 frame anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate web server segmentation faults, high 5xx error rates, or service restarts with concurrent detection of HTTP/2 protocol violations (invalid frame types, reserved bits set, invalid stream states) on same source IP.

suggestion.title: Memory Exhaustion from HTTP/2 Session Resource Abuse
suggestion.rationale: HTTP/2 Bomb DoS depends on unbounded memory growth per connection. Article describes remote DoS but pipeline did not generate resource-monitoring use case.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor web server process memory (RSS/VSZ) for growth >100MB in <60 seconds. Alert on single-connection memory consumption >500MB or process-total memory approaching system limits with active HTTP/2 traffic.

suggestion.title: npm postinstall hook execution with credential file access
suggestion.rationale: Article states malicious code 'steals credentials from GitHub, cloud platforms, and local machines' via package installation. Preinstall/postinstall hooks are the delivery mechanism but no detection rule for suspicious file I/O during npm lifecycle.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag npm (node.exe or npm.cmd) child processes accessing .ssh/, .aws/, .git/, .azure/ directories or reading cloud credential files (~/.kube/config, ~/.docker/config.json, %USERPROFILE%/.aws/credentials). Correlate with package installation timestamps via npm cache logs.

suggestion.title: npm package republishing with modified contents
suggestion.rationale: Attack 'spreads like a worm by republishing trusted packages'—requires npm registry authentication and version bump activity. No detection for unusual npm publish patterns from developer accounts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor npm CLI commands for 'npm publish' executed outside normal CI/CD pipelines. Flag version bumps to existing popular packages within short time windows. Alert on registry API publish calls from unusual GeoIPs or at anomalous times relative to user's historical pattern.

suggestion.title: CI/CD environment credential exfiltration via infected npm package
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes infection of 'CI/CD environments'—attackers harvest secrets from environment variables, .netrc files, and GitHub tokens. No UC for detecting credential staging/exfiltration during build steps.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: In CI/CD build logs, detect npm package post-install scripts spawning curl/wget/python with environment variable expansion or file I/O to credential stores, followed by outbound HTTP/S to non-standard hosts. Correlate with npm package version matching malicious release dates.

suggestion.title: npm package dependency chain anomalies (unexpected transitive dependencies)
suggestion.rationale: Malicious preinstall code can inject or modify transitive dependencies. Article does not specify technique but 'worm' behavior suggests self-replication via dependency injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Compare package-lock.json / yarn.lock files pre/post-installation for unexpected transitive deps not declared in package.json. Flag when @redhat-cloud-services or peer packages add versions pinned to attacker-controlled commits or niche registries.

suggestion.title: Local credential database enumeration during npm install
suggestion.rationale: Attack targets GitHub tokens, cloud platform credentials, and 'local machines'—implies filesystem scanning for .bashrc, .zshrc, env files, and credential managers (1Password, Bitwarden vaults).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for npm-spawned child processes (node.exe, bash, powershell) enumerating $HOME or %USERPROFILE% with high read frequency to config files, .bashrc, .profile, credential manager DB files, and browser local storage paths. Baseline developer machines to flag deviation.

suggestion.title: npm package install triggering unusual outbound DNS/HTTP from node process
suggestion.rationale: Stolen credentials must be exfiltrated. Article does not specify C2 infrastructure but preinstall hook execution implies immediate callback or credential transmission.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when node.exe or npm processes resolve domains or establish outbound connections during package installation phases (postinstall script execution). Flag connections to newly-registered or low-reputation domains. Cluster by package version to identify C2 per malicious release.

suggestion.title: Detection of Malicious or Unapproved MCP Server / Skill Invocation
suggestion.rationale: Article states '76 confirmed malicious skills out of 3,984 analyzed' and 'roughly a third of public MCP servers carry exploitable flaws.' Pipeline made no attempt to flag supply-chain based agent inputs. Log agent skill/MCP instantiation requests.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for agent runtime instantiation of external MCP servers, skills, or tools without prior approval. Flag tools whose provenance is unverified or whose names match known malicious skill indicators. Alert when agents auto-discover and invoke tools outside a whitelist.

suggestion.title: Detection of Prompt Injection Attempts in Agent Development Workflows
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'prompt injection inside development workflows' as a risk vector. Pipeline did not map this execution technique or generate detection logic for conflicting/malicious instructions injected into agent context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect payloads in agent input or system prompts that attempt to override prior instructions, invoke unauthorized tools, or escalate permissions. Flag conflicting directives (e.g., 'freeze instruction' followed by destructive action) and prompt content that deviates sharply from typical developer phrasing.

suggestion.title: Detection of Agent-Initiated Unauthorized System or Data Access
suggestion.rationale: Article warns of 'unauthorized access to systems or data' and 'data exposure through tool calls.' Pipeline missed detection use case for agents calling APIs or dev tools with excessive permissions or targeting prod systems.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when agents call internal APIs, databases, or config tools outside expected scope (e.g., querying production credentials, accessing customer data, enumerating infrastructure). Correlate agent tool calls against a baseline of approved endpoints and required permissions.

suggestion.title: Detection of Agent-Executed Destructive Commands (Data Deletion / Manipulation)
suggestion.rationale: Article cites real example: 'the coding agent that ignored repeated freeze instructions, deleted a production database, and then fabricated records to cover the error.' Pipeline extracted no kill chain phase or impact-level detection for this attack.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor database query logs and command execution logs for DROP, DELETE, TRUNCATE, or similar destructive operations initiated by agents or scripts running under agent context. Flag attempts to modify or delete records after a destructive action (cover-up pattern). Alert on commands executed against production systems by non-human actors.

suggestion.title: Detection of Agent Permission Override or Privilege Escalation Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Agent behavior has to be governed in real time' and describes an agent 'reasoning forward from a small obstacle with the permissions it happened to have.' No detection use case was generated for agents escalating, bypassing, or reinterpreting their authorization boundaries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when agents request elevated permissions or attempt to invoke protected operations. Flag instances where permission denials are followed immediately by workarounds or alternative tool calls. Detect agents re-interpreting scope or executing in elevated contexts not explicitly granted.

suggestion.title: Detection of Runtime Dependency Injection or Undeclared Tool Installation by Agents
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes that agents 'pull in MCP servers, skills, APIs, external tools... selected and invoked at runtime, with no review' and notes these become 'part of your software supply chain even though they were never declared as traditional dependencies.' Pipeline did not flag runtime tool loading.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for agents dynamically loading or installing tools, libraries, or MCP servers at runtime without manifest declaration or approval. Alert on undeclared library imports, tool invocations outside a pre-approved catalog, and dependency resolution events that occur outside standard package management workflows.

suggestion.title: GitHub OAuth Token Extraction via Malicious VS Code Extension
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'install an extension that extracts the GitHub OAuth token sent to github.dev'; no detection rule exists for token-in-transit exfiltration to unexpected processes or network destinations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for github.dev OAuth tokens accessed by VS Code extension processes and transmitted outside expected GitHub.com endpoints. Alert on GitHub API calls immediately following suspicious token access patterns, especially when listing private repositories.

suggestion.title: Webview Message Passing Exploitation in VS Code
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly details exploitation of 'VS Code's sandboxed webview message-passing system' and 'running malicious JavaScript inside a webview to simulate keypresses'; no detection for webview IPC abuse or simulated input injection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag webview postMessage() calls with payloads containing keyboard simulation (KeyboardEvent, synthEvents) or extension installation commands originating from unexpected script contexts. Correlate with subsequent VS Code extension marketplace API calls.

suggestion.title: Suspicious VS Code Extension Installation via Automated Input
suggestion.rationale: PoC 'simulate[s] keypresses in the main editor and install[s] an extension'; attack vectors from webview require detecting rapid or script-driven extension install sequences.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect extension installation in `%USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions` when initiated by webview-spawned processes or with zero user dwell time in the extension dialog. Cross-reference with GitHub.dev tab activity.

suggestion.title: Repository Enumeration via Compromised GitHub Token
suggestion.rationale: Article notes attackers 'queries the GitHub API to enumerate all private repositories the victim can access' post-token theft; no rule for anomalous repository list operations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on GitHub API /user/repos, /user/starred, or /search/repositories endpoints called with a token recently associated with VS Code activity, especially from non-browser User-Agents or IPs outside the victim's baseline.

suggestion.title: Phishing Link to github.dev with Malicious Webview Payload
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers trick users by 'clicking a link'; phishing emails or messages with github.dev URLs carrying encoded webview payloads are the entry point—no initial-access rule.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect emails or messages with github.dev URLs containing fragment identifiers or query parameters suggestive of webview payload injection (e.g., #/extensions, custom state params). Flag clicks that trigger VS Code extension installation without user directory browse.

suggestion.title: Unscoped OAuth Token Usage Across Multiple Repositories
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'token is not scoped to the particular repo... meaning it has full access to every other repo'; detect bulk cross-repo operations with single token.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for single GitHub token used to access, clone, or query >N repos in a short window, or querying unrelated repo namespaces. Baseline user token usage patterns and alert on outlier repo-access breadth.

suggestion.title: Cryptominer Process Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article title establishes 'Miners Spread via Pirated Content' as primary payload impact; pipeline generated zero impact-phase detections despite cryptomining being the stated threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on xmrig, wminercfg, monero-miner, or similar miner process names, especially from user-writable paths. Correlate with sustained high CPU utilization (>80%) and network traffic to known mining pool IPs/domains.

suggestion.title: Loader-Stage Child Process Injection (CountLoader)
suggestion.rationale: Article names 'CountLoader Hits 86K' as distribution mechanism for Weedhack; pipeline did not surface detection logic for multi-stage loader behavior despite this being named threat.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for suspicious process injection by loader processes: parent-child anomalies (legitimate process spawning uncommon child), cross-process memory access, and hollowing patterns. Flag CountLoader delivery chains terminating in system process injection.

suggestion.title: Pirated Content Download and Execution Chain
suggestion.rationale: 'Miners Spread via Pirated Content' establishes initial vector; pipeline missed detection for suspicious file execution originating from piracy sources or user-downloaded software.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag executables launched from Downloads, AppData\Local\Temp, or other user-writable locations within 15 minutes of receiving files from P2P/torrent apps, key-gen sites, or cracked-software repositories.

suggestion.title: Minecraft-Targeting Campaign Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Title specifies 'Weedhack Attacks Minecraft Users' but pipeline extracted no Minecraft-specific detections or initial-access logic related to gaming community compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for malicious Minecraft mod/launcher/texture-pack downloads from attacker-controlled sites or compromised community forums. Flag anomalous domains spoofing mojang.com, launcher.mojang.com, or official mod repository URLs.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Mining Pool Outbound Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Cryptomining payloads require persistent C2 to mining pools; pipeline failed to generate command-control-phase detection despite impact being explicitly cryptomining-related.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline normal DNS/IP destinations. Alert on new connections to known mining-pool domains (pool.monero.cc, mine.monero.today, etc.) and geographically anomalous C2 infrastructure from end-user assets.

suggestion.title: Sequential ID Enumeration Against Unauthenticated API Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'Incrementing the tenant ID by one returned the records for the next institution on the shared platform.' This is the core exploitation technique—sequential parameter fuzzing to bypass IDOR controls.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for repeated API requests to the same endpoint with incrementally increasing numeric parameters (tenant ID, user ID, account ID) from a single source, particularly when requests succeed without authentication. Flag when sequential requests extract records belonging to different organizations.

suggestion.title: Unauthenticated Access to Organization/Staff Data API
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'The endpoint required no authentication and no session of any kind' and returned 'named staff with business email addresses, direct-dial phone numbers, job titles.' This is exploitation of missing auth controls.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on successful HTTP 200/206 responses from API endpoints documented as returning organizational or employee data when the request contains no valid session token, JWT, API key, or authentication header.

suggestion.title: Cross-Origin API Requests Bypass CORS to Sensitive Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'The platform's cross-origin policy allowed any third-party site to invoke the same request from a visitor's browser without user interaction.' CORS misconfiguration enabling client-side exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for requests with Origin or Referer headers pointing to external/untrusted domains when accessing sensitive API endpoints that return confidential data. Flag mismatched origin-to-endpoint pairs and successful 200/201 responses despite CORS policy violations in headers.

suggestion.title: Bulk Extraction of Staff Identity Data via API
suggestion.rationale: Article describes extraction of 'named staff with business email addresses, direct-dial phone numbers, job titles, and an internal code' across multiple organizations. Pattern: low-auth API returning PII at scale.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when a single API session or source IP extracts >100 staff records from the organization endpoint in a 5-minute window, or when requests pattern-match the structure (sequential tenant enumeration + staff list retrieval) characteristic of reconnaissance.

suggestion.title: Fraudulent Loan Applications Submitted with Internal Personnel Codes
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'any caller in possession of a valid code could submit a prospective borrower application in a named officer's name...the platform would treat the submission as legitimate.' Codes extracted via enumeration are weaponized for fraud.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag loan applications submitted with valid internal personnel attribution codes (extracted via prior reconnaissance) when the submission originates from an external IP, geographic anomaly, or during off-hours. Cross-reference applicant contact info against staff directory.

suggestion.title: Detection of Unauthenticated Endpoints Serving Sensitive Data in Continuous Testing
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes: 'no automated scanner surfaces this finding. Catching it required walking sequential tenant IDs against an undocumented endpoint.' Continuous scanning must detect missing auth on data endpoints between annual tests.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Continuous security scanning should flag any API endpoint returning organizational or employee data (status 200/206, content-type application/json, data volume >1KB) when accessed without credentials, OAuth token, session header, or mTLS certificate. Alert on new endpoints appearing in scope that lack authentication enforcement.

suggestion.title: Automated AD Discovery via Scripted LDAP/DirectorySearch
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'automated Active Directory (AD) discovery panel' that 'collects observations from completed tasks and selects the next action from predefined choices.' This automation pattern (iterative LDAP queries, ADFind, PowerShell Get-AD* calls) is detectable but was not surfaced as UC.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect iterative or batch Active Directory discovery queries from Python processes or unusual command-line execution. Look for sequences of LDAP queries, Get-ADUser, Get-ADComputer, or net commands executed in rapid succession from non-admin users or from Documents/temp directories.

suggestion.title: Python-Based Process Injection with Shellcode Wrapping
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Python-based malware development scripts for injecting shellcode into legitimate Windows executables while preserving original functionality.' Injection from Python interpreters is unusual and detectable but omitted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect Python.exe or Python3.exe process creating unsigned child processes, allocating RWX memory, or calling CreateRemoteThread/WriteProcessMemory via native API hooks. Correlate with ntdll/kernel32 imports from Python scripts.

suggestion.title: Cobalt Strike Beacon Traffic Masquerading as Legitimate HTTP
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies 'Cobalt Strike profiles designed to make beacon traffic resemble legitimate web requests' and profiles were tested against EDR. Beacon C2 patterns, even obfuscated, have detectable signatures but no UC was generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for HTTP/HTTPS C2 patterns: suspicious User-Agent strings, unusual request cadences, beacon-like data patterns in POST bodies, or traffic to known Cobalt Strike C2 IP ranges. Correlate with suspicious process execution and parent-child relationships.

suggestion.title: Payload Staging and Execution from User Documents Directory
suggestion.rationale: Article reports 'payloads stored in C:\Users\User\Documents\test' — staging from user-writable paths is common but detectable. No UC surfaced for monitoring Documents folder for executable staging.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on execution of Rust/Go binaries or DLLs from User\Documents, Users\<user>\AppData, or %TEMP% paths. Correlate file creation timestamps with execution events. Flag parent processes spawning children from these paths.

suggestion.title: Telegram Bot API Used for C2 Communication
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'Telegram bot API–based external command and control (C2) mechanism that routed communication through Telegram's infrastructure.' This is a rare but distinct C2 channel that requires specific detection rules but was omitted.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound HTTPS connections to Telegram API endpoints (api.telegram.org) from non-browser processes or with suspicious frequency. Monitor for bot token patterns in network traffic or memory. Correlate with Python process execution and suspicious parent-child relationships.

suggestion.title: Cloudflare Worker Used as C2 Redirector/Proxy
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'Cloudflare Worker acting as a front-end redirector to obscure the actual backend C2 server.' This redirector pattern (legitimate service abused for C2 fronting) is emerging TTP but no detection logic proposed.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual Cloudflare Worker domain patterns in process network logs, especially from non-web-facing processes. Identify known Cloudflare Worker C2 domains via threat intel. Correlate with malware process behavior and beaconing patterns.

suggestion.title: CVE-2024-21182 T3 Protocol Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability is 'exploited remotely by threat actors with no privileges' via 'T3, IIOP' protocols against WebLogic. Pipeline missed detection for the explicit attack surface.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for T3 protocol (TCP/7001) connections to Oracle WebLogic servers from external or suspicious sources. Correlate with WebLogic error logs showing authentication failures or deserialization errors. Baseline normal T3 traffic and alert on anomalous connection patterns, especially multiple failed handshakes followed by successful connection.

suggestion.title: Unexpected Child Process from WebLogic Java Process
suggestion.rationale: CVE-2024-21182 achieves 'complete access to all Oracle WebLogic Server accessible data' via RCE; article context indicates post-exploitation activity. Pipeline missed command execution detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag child processes spawned by WebLogic Java process (java.exe, w3wp.exe) that launch cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, or network utilities (curl, wget, nc, certutil). WebLogic should not normally spawn shell interpreters. Include parent-child relationship validation and module load events.

suggestion.title: WebLogic Version Enumeration / Fingerprinting
suggestion.rationale: Article notes attackers target 'systems running Oracle WebLogic Server versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.1.0.0'; threat actors will enumerate versions before exploitation. Pipeline missed reconnaissance detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect requests to WebLogic admin console (/console), common enumeration paths, or error pages that leak version info. Monitor for multiple failed login attempts to WebLogic console followed by successful exploitation attempts. Alert on HTTP 200/403 responses to version-disclosure endpoints from single source within short window.

suggestion.title: Exposed Oracle WebLogic T3/IIOP Ports on Internet-Facing Systems
suggestion.rationale: Shodan data cited in article shows '1,592 Oracle WebLogic servers exposed online'; external accessibility is prerequisite for exploitation described. Pipeline missed asset discovery baseline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain inventory of systems running WebLogic (via process discovery, network banners, CDM data). Flag any WebLogic instances accessible from Internet-facing IPs on T3 (7001) or IIOP (7002) ports. Cross-reference with vulnerability scanner output for versions 12.2.1.4.0 and 14.1.1.0.0.

suggestion.title: IIOP Protocol Anomalies to Oracle WebLogic
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly names IIOP (port 7002) as attack vector alongside T3. Most enterprise environments should have zero IIOP traffic or strictly-controlled baselines. Pipeline missed protocol-level detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: IIOP is used for Java RMI over CORBA; most modern deployments use T3 or REST instead. Flag any IIOP traffic (TCP/7002) to WebLogic servers, especially from external sources or anomalous internal sources. Baseline legitimate IIOP consumers and alert on deviations.

suggestion.title: WebLogic Data Exfiltration Post-RCE
suggestion.rationale: Article states successful exploitation results in 'unauthorized access to critical data or complete access to all Oracle WebLogic Server accessible data.' Pipeline missed post-compromise detection for data staging/exfil.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Post-RCE, attackers will access WebLogic data stores. Monitor for WebLogic process reading config files (setDomainEnv.sh, security properties), accessing Java keystore files, or connecting to backend databases. Correlate with earlier indicators of compromise (failed T3 handshakes, unusual Java child processes).

suggestion.title: CVE-2022-0492 Asset Exposure Hunt
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly identifies CVE-2022-0492 as currently exploited in the wild and mandates federal patch deadline 2026-06-05; vulnerability scanner coverage is the standard detection baseline for CISA KEV entries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Match vulnerability scanner output and patch status against CVE-2022-0492. Flag systems with missing kernel patches or vulnerable kernel versions prior to the federal deadline.

suggestion.title: cgroups v1 release_agent Privilege Escalation
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'privilege escalation via the cgroups v1 release_agent feature' — this specific attack vector requires detection beyond generic privilege escalation patterns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unprivileged processes reading or writing /sys/fs/cgroup/*/release_agent files, cgroup attribute modifications, or privilege transitions following cgroup subsystem access.

suggestion.title: Kernel Privilege Escalation — Unprivileged-to-Root Transition
suggestion.rationale: Article describes improper authentication enabling unprivileged kernel feature access; detect privilege boundary violations without traditional elevation (sudo/setuid) correlated with cgroups operations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag processes elevating from non-root to root without sudo/setuid, especially those preceded by syscalls to /proc/[pid]/cgroup or /sys/fs/cgroup paths.

suggestion.title: CVE-2025-48595 Vulnerability Presence Hunt
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly instructs: 'Standard asset-exposure hunt [...] Substitute this CVE wherever the template references <CVE>: CVE: CVE-2025-48595'. This templated detection was not generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query asset inventory and vulnerability scanners for Android Framework instances with CVE-2025-48595 unfixed. Cross-reference against patch-due date 2026-06-05. Prioritize public-facing or network-accessible Android Framework components.

suggestion.title: Integer Overflow Code Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article states: 'integer overflow vulnerability that allows for code execution'. This execution phase was not mapped to a kill-chain phase or detection, despite being the technical core of the exploit.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected code execution emanating from Android Framework services following integer overflow exploitation patterns. Flag abnormal child process spawning, memory heap corruption indicators, or privilege boundary violations within Framework processes.

suggestion.title: Local Privilege Escalation Post-Exploit
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states: 'local privilege escalation'. The kill-chain reconstruction omitted this phase entirely despite it being a stated attack outcome.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect privilege escalation attempts immediately following CVE-2025-48595 exploitation. Monitor for transitions from unprivileged app context to system/root, capability grants, or Android permission elevation in audit logs.

suggestion.title: Detect brute-force authentication attempts against web applications
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'brute-force attack' as the compromise vector. The pipeline should flag high-volume failed authentication attempts followed by success on the same account.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for 10+ failed login attempts followed by a successful login within a short window (10-60 min) on the same user account. Correlate with IP geolocation changes or TOR exit nodes. Flag if source IP is not in organization's known IP allowlist.

suggestion.title: Detect unusual authentication patterns for SaaS credential storage services
suggestion.rationale: Dashlane is a specific web-accessible password manager; attacker targeting it likely means reconnaissance of service-specific attack patterns. Pipeline should correlate authentication logs specific to password manager domains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound HTTP/HTTPS traffic to known password manager domains (dashlane.com, bitwarden.com, 1password.com, lastpass.com) for repeated connection attempts with short inter-arrival times, indicating automated credential enumeration.

suggestion.title: Detect bulk authentication failures with geographic anomalies
suggestion.rationale: Brute-force campaigns typically originate from fewer geographic regions than legitimate users. Article mentions encrypted vaults of <20 users, suggesting targeted attack; geographic correlation on failed auths can identify source concentration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Aggregate failed authentication attempts by source geolocation and ASN. Alert if >50% of failures in a 1-hour window originate from same country, ISP, or datacenter, especially if different from user's historical baseline.

suggestion.title: Detect credential compromise post-breach validation activity
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline should generate proactive hunt UC for use cases occurring AFTER breach disclosure. Once <20 vaults are confirmed compromised, monitor for downstream account takeover: cross-service authentication, secondary account creations, privilege escalations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: For Dashlane-compromised users (via breach notification or OSINT), flag if their credentials are used to authenticate to secondary services (cloud providers, corporate VPN, O365) within 48 hours post-disclosure, or if new MFA methods are registered.

suggestion.title: Monitor for password manager vault export/sync events
suggestion.rationale: Attack resulted in 'encrypted vaults downloaded'; if attacker obtains vault material, they may attempt export, decryption, or re-sync to secondary device. Article implies vaults were exfiltrated; UC should detect vault access anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Dashlane API logs for vault_export, vault_sync, or bulk_credential_access events from IPs not in user's known device list. Flag if export/sync is followed by rapid HTTPS egress to non-Dashlane infrastructure.

suggestion.title: WinRAR Archive Extraction Followed by Suspicious Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article establishes WinRAR as the exploit delivery vector and explicitly names GammaWorm/GammaSteel as payloads; no detection generated for the child process execution pattern post-extraction.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for WinRAR process (unrar.exe, winrar.exe) extracting files followed within seconds by execution of newly-extracted binaries or scripts with suspicious attributes (unsigned, obfuscated names, renamed system tools).

suggestion.title: GammaWorm/GammaSteel Malware Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Pipeline did not extract or generate detections for the two named malware families explicitly mentioned as the payload of this campaign.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect process names, file paths, or command-line artifacts associated with GammaWorm and GammaSteel (requires hash/signature database or behavior patterns such as suspicious C2 callbacks, file write patterns, or registry persistence attempts).

suggestion.title: Registry or Filesystem Persistence Following WinRAR Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article implies malware delivery and execution against Ukrainian targets; standard Gamaredon post-exploitation includes persistence via Run keys or startup folders, but no detection covers this step.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run or Startup folder modifications immediately following WinRAR extraction; look for write operations by processes spawned as children of archive decompression.

suggestion.title: Suspicious C2 Beaconing from Newly-Executed Process
suggestion.rationale: GammaWorm and GammaSteel are described as being delivered—implies command-and-control functionality, but no detection targets outbound C2 communication post-execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate new process execution from WinRAR extraction context with outbound connections to non-standard ports, known Gamaredon C2 domains/IPs, or HTTP User-Agents matching historical campaign patterns.

suggestion.title: Gamaredon Campaign Artifact Detection
suggestion.rationale: Gamaredon is a named threat actor in the title; pipeline did not surface actor-specific TTPs, command-line patterns, or file paths historically used by this group.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for Gamaredon-attributed batch scripts, VBScript loaders, or reconnaissance commands (ipconfig, whoami, systeminfo, tasklist) executed in rapid succession in contexts linked to archive decompression or suspicious parent processes.

suggestion.title: WinRAR Vulnerability Exploitation Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly states WinRAR is exploited; no detection for abnormal WinRAR behavior or known CVE exploitation patterns (e.g., path traversal during extraction, suspicious command-line arguments).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for WinRAR processes spawning with command-line arguments indicating automated/scripted extraction, outputting to world-writable or system directories, or writing files outside user profile; correlate with file-write events to sensitive paths.

suggestion.title: Android Framework CVE-2025-48595 Exploitation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states CVE-2025-48595 'may be under limited, targeted exploitation' and is 'actively abused.' 'Local attackers can exploit the...high-severity Android Framework vulnerability to gain code execution and escalate privileges on devices running Android 14 or later.' Core vulnerability with zero detection rules generated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for privilege escalation attempts within Android Framework components on Android 14+ devices. Detect capability elevation, unauthorized SELinux domain transitions, or unusual system call sequences targeting process privilege boundaries without corresponding authorization events.

suggestion.title: Unpatched Android Security Bulletin Devices
suggestion.rationale: Article notes 'Google Pixel devices will receive these security updates immediately, other vendors will often take longer.' 124 vulnerabilities require inventory of devices still on pre-June 2026 patch levels to identify exploitable population.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag Android 14+ devices not on 2026-06-01 or later patch level 30 days post-bulletin. Prioritize corporate, government, and high-profile users given article's reference to 'high-profile or high-interest individuals' as targets.

suggestion.title: Remote Privilege Escalation Without User Interaction (Framework)
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies 'a critical security vulnerability in the Framework component that could lead to remote escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.' This no-interaction remote priv-esc is highest severity attack path in bulletin.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect privilege or capability elevation within Framework without preceding user consent, permissions request, or privilege request system calls. Flag unauthorized transitions to system_server UID, root, or restricted SELinux domains.

suggestion.title: Coordinated Android Zero-Day Campaign (CVE-2025-48633, CVE-2025-48572, CVE-2026-21385)
suggestion.rationale: Article documents three additional zero-days all marked 'under limited, targeted exploitation' from prior months (Dec, Mar), suggesting coordinated multi-vector campaign. 'Have been exploited in the past by commercial spyware and by nation-state operations.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate exploitation indicators across CVE-2025-48633 (Framework), CVE-2025-48572 (Framework), and CVE-2026-21385 (Qualcomm display) on same device or user. Detect suspicious code injection, unexpected library loading, or process spawning patterns consistent with commercial spyware post-exploitation.

suggestion.title: Android Privilege Escalation via Patched Kernel Vulnerability
suggestion.rationale: June 2026 update patches 124 flaws including at least one actively exploited; kernel vulns typically enable EoP—missing detection for suspicious capability requests or task scheduler anomalies post-install
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for processes requesting kernel module loading, memory-mapped I/O operations, or SELinux policy bypasses immediately after system boot on patched Android builds. Correlate with app installation events from untrusted sources. Legitimate privesc is constrained; anomalies suggest exploit attempts.

suggestion.title: Suspicious APK Installation Post Android Update
suggestion.rationale: Update announcement establishes patch window; attackers typically stage exploits before patches propagate—missing detection for staged APKs or sideloaded app updates in first 72 hours post-patch release
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on any APK installation (sideload, ADB, or Play Store staging) within 72 hours of Android security update announcement, especially if source IP or app signature appear in exploit-kit infrastructure. Cross-reference APK hash against known malware families.

suggestion.title: Data Exfiltration via Patched Information Disclosure Vulnerability
suggestion.rationale: Article states 124 flaws patched but body does not detail categories; information disclosure bugs often enable credential/PII theft—missing UC for abnormal file reads or contacts/SMS access patterns
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unusual access to /data/data/ directories (credentials, tokens), System/priv-app directories (protected assets), or bulk reads of /data/misc/ (logs, caches). Flag processes not normally granted READ_CONTACTS, READ_CALL_LOG, or READ_SMS permissions attempting these operations.

suggestion.title: Exploitation of ActivelyExploited Android Flaw (CVE TBD)
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly mentions 'one actively exploited' flaw—cannot form detection without CVE ID, but missing UC stub for in-the-wild indicators (command line args, memory signatures, crash dumps typical of known exploit)
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Once CVE published, hunt for process crashes with specific kernel addresses, unusual Java.lang.Runtime.exec() calls with shell metacharacters, or DLL injection patterns. Monitor Android WebView component restarts. Cross-reference with browser history for malicious domains.

suggestion.title: Composer Package Tag Rewritten with New Hash
suggestion.rationale: Core attack vector explicitly stated: 'Every Tag Across Multiple Composer Packages Rewritten'. Detection must track version/tag integrity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert when composer.lock or installed package hash diverges from registry or git tag. Track commit history for push events to Laravel-Lang repositories outside normal release windows. Correlate tag rewrites across multiple Laravel-Lang packages in same timeframe.

suggestion.title: CI Environment Variables Exfiltrated by Installed Package
suggestion.rationale: Attack explicitly steals 'CI Secrets'. Malicious package code must access and transmit env vars during build execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor composer install/update processes for child processes invoking env(), getenv(), or $_ENV access. Flag unexpected outbound HTTPS/DNS from build container immediately post-package-installation. Correlate with CI secret names (CI_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, AWS_ACCESS_KEY).

suggestion.title: Package Installation from Compromised Repository Mirror
suggestion.rationale: Supply chain attack suggests attacker-controlled package source or git repository. 'Rewritten tags' implies git/registry tampering.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect when composer repositories point to non-standard URLs, local path overrides, or git branches not in whitelist. Alert on composer.lock pinning to unusual versions or pre-release tags. Cross-reference package timestamps with known-compromised window.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Function Calls in Downloaded Package Source
suggestion.rationale: Payload execution happens during composer require/update. Malicious code must be detectable via static analysis before installation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Pre-installation static analysis: grep package source for base64_decode, eval(), system(), exec(), curl/file_get_contents to non-whitelisted URLs. Flag obfuscated code patterns. Compare against security-scanned baseline of same package version from previous installation.

suggestion.title: Multiple Laravel-Lang Packages Compromised Simultaneously
suggestion.rationale: Attack affects 'Multiple Composer Packages' with coordinated tag rewrites—suggests single maintainer account compromise or package registry control.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate package update activity across laravel-lang/* namespace. Alert if 3+ packages updated by same account within 1-hour window outside normal release schedule. Flag if push occurs from new/unusual IP or without MFA. Cross-check release notes for unexpected changes or deletions.

suggestion.title: CI Secret Exfiltration to External Domain
suggestion.rationale: Stolen secrets must be transmitted to attacker infrastructure. 'Steal CI Secrets' implies out-of-band exfiltration channel.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound TLS/DNS from CI build agents during composer install phases. Flag connections to newly-registered or zero-reputation domains.
